title: Underlying Mechanisms of Helicobacter pylori in Caries Progression and the Corresponding Dual‐Responsive Hydrogel‐Based Intervention
abstract: ABSTRACT Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infects nearly half of the global population. Given that H. pylori is considered poorly adapted to the oral environment, previous studies have mainly focused on gastric infection. By contrast, how H. pylori persists in the oral cavity and relates to oral diseases remains unclear. This study investigates the role of H. pylori in caries progression. The results show that H. pylori is retained within Streptococcus mutans ( S. mutans ) biofilms, and its presence is associated with transcriptional remodeling in S. mutans , alongside increased overall cariogenic potential of the mixed biofilm. In a rat caries model, H. pylori co‐colonization aggravates caries progression and oral microbiota dysbiosis. To address this pathological niche, a multifunctional hydrogel, termed GPAM, is designed by integrating a Cu 2 O@Pt heterojunction (MCP) with amorphous calcium phosphate (ACP). Under activation by yellow light and ultrasound, MCP generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) to disrupt S. mutans–H. pylori mixed biofilms. Meanwhile, released Cu 2+ reduces H. pylori urease activity, and ACP promotes tooth remineralization. GPAM also shows microbiota‐modulating potential. Together, these findings provide insight into H. pylori ‐associated caries progression and support GPAM as a multifunctional therapeutic strategy for mixed biofilms and caries‐related damage.

title: Strengthening TMP‐Derived Phosphate SEI via Sn Scaffold and BF 4 − Interphase Chemistry for Ultra‐Stable, High‐Rate Zn Metal Anodes
abstract: ABSTRACT While dynamic solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) construction and solvation engineering have transformed aqueous zinc‐ion batteries, translating these approaches to Organic electrolytes (OE) remains a challenging endeavor due to fundamentally different interfacial environments, solvation thermodynamics, and anion decomposition pathways. Despite providing superior thermodynamic stabilization to Zn anode, OE exhibits low ionic conductivity, thereby limiting operational current densities. Herein, we report the first demonstration of Sn(BF 4 ) 2 /H 2 O (SFB) additive integration in a non‐flammable trimethyl phosphate (TMP)‐ethanol (EtOH) (2:1 v/v) OE to architect a gradient SEI interphase on Zn anodes. The multifunctional integration of SFB facilitates the formation of a Sn‐coated Zn surface, a BF 4 1− ‐derived SEI@Zn, and H 2 O molecules as a proton source, collectively contributing to enhanced capacity. This strategic solvent‐salt‐metal synergy enables bi‐layered interfacial engineering within a single electrolyte system, significantly improving the reversibility and stability of the Zn anode. Consequently, SFB enables a robust SEI, achieving exceptional Zn anode durability (7000 h), high‐rate capability (10 mA cm −2 ), and a high Coulombic efficiency (CE) of 99.8%. Full cells with SFB outperform controls in coin and pouch configurations. Given the rarity of additive(s) in OEs, this study offers a new path to boost stability and lifespan of non‐aqueous Zn batteries.

title: Chemical Coordination and Pore Confinement Enabling a Bifunctional Interface for Accelerated Desolvation and Oriented Deposition Toward Stable Zinc Metal Anodes
abstract: ABSTRACT Aqueous zinc‐ion batteries show great potential for large‐scale energy storage; however, dendrites formation and corrosion on zinc anodes significantly hinder their practical applications. Uneven Zn deposition leads to dendrite growth, while H 2 O molecules in solvated Zn 2+ ions exacerbate surface corrosion and the hydrogen evolution reaction. Herein, we propose a Schiff‐base‐covalently‐grafted UiO‐66‐NH 2 metal‐organic framework to construct a bifunctional interface for stable zinc metal anodes. Specifically, the chemical chelation between Schiff base and Zn 2+ accelerates desolvation and suppresses side reactions. Meanwhile, the uniformly distributed Zn 2+ ‐chelated sites and the well‐defined confined pore channels of UiO‐66‐NH 2 scaffold guide a homogeneous Zn 2+ flux and promote Zn(002)‐oriented deposition. As a result, this bifunctional interface enables Zn plating/stripping with a high Coulombic efficiency of 99.8% over 2000 cycles at 5 mA cm −2 /1 mAh cm −2 . Furthermore, it achieves a capacity retention of over 90% after 4000 charge–discharge cycles in a Zn||MnO 2 full cell. This work is expected to open a new avenue for interfacial chemical regulation toward stabilizing zinc metal anodes.

title: Synchronous and Unidirectional Epitaxy of Layer‐Controlled Graphene on Oxidized Single‐Crystal Copper Wafers With Tunable Stacking Order
abstract: ABSTRACT The deterministic synthesis of wafer‐scale two‐dimensional (2D) materials with programmable layer number, crystallographic orientation, and stacking order is essential for unlocking their layer‐dependent quantum properties and enabling scalable device integration. Here, we demonstrate a synchronous and unidirectional epitaxy strategy for chemical vapor deposition growth of layer‐controlled graphene on atomically flat oxidized single‐crystal Cu wafers. Using a Cu(111)–Cu 2 O(111) heterogeneous catalytic substrate, we achieved 2‐inch single‐crystalline graphene films with precisely tunable layer numbers (2 to 5). By engineering the atomic steps of high‐index Cu surfaces, we created deterministic spatial patterning of alternating Bernal and rhombohedral stacking in trilayer graphene, as confirmed by near‐field nano‐optics and angle‐resolved photoemission spectroscopy. The resulting wafer‐scale films exhibit exceptional thickness uniformity, high crystallinity, and an ultra‐flat surface. This work provides a unified growth framework that concurrently resolves the intertwined challenges of layer control, wafer‐scale single crystallinity, and stacking order modulation, laying a material foundation for advanced device studies and potential applications.

title: Dead Cell‐Based Carriers: Strategies, Biomedical Applications, and Prospects
abstract: ABSTRACT Living cells have been explored for drug delivery due to their active motility and homing ability; however, their potential toxicity, uncontrolled proliferation, and poor stability severely hinder their practical application and clinical translation. In recent years, dead cells have emerged as promising delivery vehicles due to their enhanced safety, improved stability, and retention of key bioactive molecules. In this review, we summarize the fabrication strategies and delivery characteristics of four types of dead carriers including microalgae, yeasts, bacteria, and mammalian cells in treating diseases such as bacterial pneumonia, inflammatory bowel disease, and cancer. We also discuss the therapeutic mechanisms of endogenous bioactive components, platform‐specific limitations, and the advantages/disadvantages of dead cell‐based carriers. Finally, we formulate general design principles for dead cell carriers and provide a forward‐looking perspective on key translational bottlenecks, including safety assessment, standardized manufacturing, and regulatory pathways, with the aim of guiding the development of safe and effective dead cell‐based delivery systems.

title: 3D Electron Diffraction Reveals Counterion Coordination in Co‐Existing Polymorphs of Ag29 Nanocluster
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT We unravel the complete structural architecture of the polymorphic Na 3 [Ag 29 (BDT) 12 (TPP) 4 ] nanocluster (NC) using three‐dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED) of microscopic crystals. By drop‐casting nanocluster solution directly onto microscopy grids, we achieve in situ crystallization of nanometer‐sized polymorphs and independently resolve co‐existing cubic and trigonal phases crystal‐by‐crystal from a single grid square. Using difference electrostatic potential (DESP) maps derived from empirical 3D ED data, we pinpoint the specific lattice locations of the elusive Na + counterions and observe distinct coordination environments across the two polymorphs. In the densely packed, solvent‐free cubic phase, Na + binds exclusively to thermodynamically favored pockets formed by one core‐anchored and two staple sulfur atoms. Conversely, within the open, solvated trigonal lattice, Na + occupies both these core‐anchored sites and alternative positions coordinated entirely by three sulfur atoms of an outer Ag 3 S 3 staple motif. These findings establish 3D ED as a powerful tool for resolving nanoscale polymorphic mixtures and demonstrate how macroscopic crystal packing influences local ionic interactions, providing key structural insights for the design of cluster‐based assemblies.

title: Phenonium‐Ion‐Mediated Skeletal Editing of Paracyclophanes
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Phenonium ions have played a central role in physical–organic chemistry, yet their use as strategic intermediates in synthesis remains underexplored. Here, we report a phenonium‐ion‐mediated strategy for the skeletal editing of paracyclophanes. Installation of a one‐carbon handle at the aliphatic bridge, followed by direct alcohol activation with BF 3 ·OEt 2 under solvolysis‐avoiding conditions, generates a paracyclophane‐derived phenonium ion that undergoes regioselective ring opening by external nucleophiles. This strategy provides modular access to functionalized higher paracyclophane homologues and tolerates S‐, N‐, C‐, selenium‐, and halide‐based nucleophiles under operationally simple, gram‐scalable conditions. The sequence can be applied iteratively and extended to double bridge expansion, while reductive desulfurization furnishes the corresponding parent hydrocarbons. Mechanistic studies combining nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, kinetic analysis, stereochemical probes, and density functional theory calculations support a self‐accelerating mechanism in which product water shifts BF 3 speciation toward BF 3 ·H 2 O, which assists leaving‐group departure through hydrogen‐bond donation and thereby facilitates phenonium‐ion formation. Together, these results establish paracyclophane‐derived phenonium ions as controllable intermediates for skeletal editing and provide practical access to higher paracyclophane topologies with application potential in functional materials, as exemplified by a bridge‐expanded thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) emitter.

title: Palladium‐Catalyzed Cross‐Coupling of Transiently Stable Heterocyclic Organolithiums
source: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT The use of organolithium reagents in cross‐coupling (the Murahashi coupling) has undergone a resurgence over the past decade, driven by the discovery that modern ligands and catalysts can promote productive couplings that outcompete common side reactions. Despite this progress, most reported methods rely on stable, well‐behaved organolithium partners such as n ‐BuLi and PhLi, leaving many synthetically valuable but highly sensitive heterocyclic organolithiums outside the practical scope. In this work, we employ high‐throughput experimentation (HTE) to identify catalytic systems that enable C─C bond formation on minute or sub‐minute time scales. These ultrafast conditions enable coupling of sensitive organolithium species, such as lithiated pyridines and quinolines, before they decompose under conventional cross‐coupling conditions. We identify several complementary, top‐performing catalyst systems that address the different challenges encountered across nucleophile–electrophile combinations, including catalyst inhibition, side reactions, and rapid organolithium decomposition. Limits of the batch protocol are identified and overcome through development of an alternative flash‐chemistry protocol that further expands the scope to organolithium reagents that decompose on time scales of seconds. Together, these studies establish a practical strategy for coupling transient heterocyclic organolithiums and substantially expand the scope of the Murahashi reaction.

title: In-Situ Removal of Sr Segregation via Surface Construction to Engineer Highly Active Oxygen Electrode for Low-Temperature Solid Oxide Electrochemical Cells Operating below 500 °C
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Recent advancements in solid oxide electrochemical cells (SOCs) heavily depend on the development of active and stable oxygen electrodes that exhibit superior activity and stability for oxygen reduction and evolution reactions at low temperatures. Here, we report a new surface-constructed oxygen electrode, Sr(Mg,Ti,Fe)O3–δ coated with Co3O4 (SMTF–Co3O4), designed to operate below 500 °C for low-temperature SOCs. The electrode electrochemical performance is primarily improved by the in situ reaction of Co3O4 with surface-segregated SrO, forming SrCoO3 and Co3O4/SrCoO3/SMTF heterointerfaces, which significantly enhances the surface oxygen adsorption capacity. The SMTF–Co3O4 electrode demonstrates a remarkably low reaction activation energy of ∼0.56 eV, with electrode polarization resistance as low as 0.56 Ω cm2 at 450 °C. The full cell, incorporating a thin scandia-stabilized zirconia (ScSz) electrolyte (∼3 μm) and the SMTF–Co3O4 oxygen electrode, reaches maximum power density and electrolysis current density (at 1.3 V) of 0.6 W/cm2 and 0.44 A/cm2, respectively, at 500 °C. Especially, 5–8 times enhancement in the cell performance at 450 °C is achieved by SMTF with the surface construction compared to the pristine electrode. Furthermore, the SMTF–Co3O4 electrode maintains stable performance in both fuel cell and electrolysis modes.

title: Nature-Inspired Directional Fluid Transport Enables Silanized Topo-Vascular Cellulose Aerogel for Efficient Oil/Water Separation
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Oil pollution from petroleum-related activities and oily industrial wastewater pose a persistent challenge to aquatic environments, motivating the development of efficient sorbent and separation materials. However, conventional aerogels usually require multistep fabrication and show limited mechanical robustness. Herein, a silanized topo-vascular cellulose aerogel (STVCA) is developed through a top-down strategy using the oriented transport architecture of Spatholobus suberectus Dunn stems as a structural template. Vapor-phase silanization tailors the cellulose interface while the processed scaffold retains key topological features of the native hierarchical vascular architecture, combining low-surface-energy chemistry with the inherited channel organization and mechanical integrity. The resulting STVCA serves as a robust, fast mass-transfer medium for oil/water separation, showing rapid oil wetting, stable hydrophobicity, and anisotropic capillary transport. Dry STVCA reaches a compressive stress of 28.41 MPa at 80% radial strain (σ80), whereas oil-loaded STVCA reaches σ80 = 27.14 MPa and retains 91% of its initial σ80 after 80 compression cycles. The cross-sectional surface and longitudinal faces have mean static water contact angles of 151.05 ± 4.01° and 143.80 ± 5.92°, while a representative internal cut-surface measurement reaches 155.7°. Owing to the preserved vascular-bundle topology, STVCA achieves anisotropic mass transfer, a chloroform uptake capacity of 11.73 ± 0.61 g·g–1, a continuous separation flux of 13126 L·m-2·h–1, and a separation efficiency of up to 99%. This biomass-derived aerogel provides a durable platform for oil-spill remediation.

title: MgH2 with a Pre-Synthesized Ti–Ni Composite Catalyst: Superior Sorption Kinetics and High Saturated Capacity over Physically Mixed Ni/Ti
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Magnesium hydride (MgH2) is a promising solid-state hydrogen storage material owing to its high theoretical capacity, earth abundance, and low cost. However, its practical application is severely hindered by sluggish sorption kinetics and high thermodynamic stability. Herein, we systematically compare the catalytic effects of elemental Ni, elemental Ti, physically mixed Ni/Ti, and a pre-synthesized Ti–Ni composite catalyst on the hydrogen storage performance of MgH2, aiming to understand the advantages and disadvantages of the catalytic performance of Ni and Ti and to exert their synergistic catalytic effect. Our results suggest that Ni is associated with faster initial hydrogenation kinetics and lower onset dehydrogenation temperatures, while Ti correlates with higher equilibrium capacities and more sustained hydrogenation/dehydrogenation behavior at elevated temperatures. These distinct catalytic tendencies are inferred from systematic comparisons of sorption kinetics, phase evolution, elemental distribution, and kinetic modeling. Simple co-doping of Ni and Ti partially combines these benefits but fails to eliminate the intrinsic drawbacks of each element. It is noteworthy that the pre-synthesized Ti–Ni composite catalyst further overcomes the above-mentioned drawbacks and exhibits a more uniform distribution of elements, which further improves both the hydrogen absorption rate and the extent of the reaction in MgH2. As a result, the MgH2–5wt%pre-Ti-Ni-c-c composite absorbs 6.10 wt % H2 within 27.3 s at 275 °C and releases 5.54 wt % H2 within 548 s at 325 °C, with a markedly reduced dehydrogenation enthalpy from 93.28 to 72.25 kJ mol–1. After 10 cycles, its hydrogen absorption and desorption capacity retentions reach 96.3 and 93.5%, respectively, demonstrating improved initial cycling stability compared with BM-MgH2 (82.6%). Mechanistic studies combining phase evolution, kinetic modeling, and DFT calculations attribute the superior performance to the combined action of three components: the NiTi bimetallic phase for a collaborative catalytic effect, reversible Mg2Ni/Mg2NiHx phases that contribute to rapid initial kinetics, and TiO2 that induces stronger lattice distortion. This work demonstrates that the pre-synthesized Ti–Ni composite catalyst, with its superior dispersion, effectively overcomes the limitations of physically mixed Ni/Ti systems and achieves a better balance between rapid initial reaction rates and deeper reactions in actual test results.

title: Phase-Transition-Driven Thermomechanical Regulation of Thermal Interfaces
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Thermal interfaces are often limited by imperfect real contact, where surface asperities and interfacial gaps can dominate the overall thermal resistance. Here, we develop a flexible phase-change composite (FPCC) that couples the solid–liquid transition of n-docosane with mechanical softening, expansion-generated normal loading, and interfacial reconfiguration to regulate thermal contact. The composite integrates n-docosane within a compliant styrene–ethylene–butylene–styrene (SEBS) matrix supported by an interconnected expanded-graphite (EG) scaffold. The optimized FPCC exhibits a thermal conductivity of 5.18 W m–1 K–1 and a latent heat of 153.5 J g–1. Across the phase transition, the tensile modulus decreases to ∼0.60 MPa, while expansion under interfacial constraint generates a normal stress exceeding 40 kPa (∼5.8 psi). An equivalent-pressure analysis based on the measured Rcontact–P relationship indicates that a pressure increment of ∼5.8 psi corresponds to an approximately 54% reduction in contact thermal resistance from the 5 psi reference condition. Frequency-domain thermoreflectance measurements further reveal an increase in effective contact conductance from 2.32 to 8.99 MW m–2 K–1 across the transition, while synchronized mechanical-thermal measurements show reproducible co-evolution of normal loading and conductance during repeated cycling. The enhanced contact state is partially retained after cooling, indicating that repeatable thermomechanical modulation operates together with partially retained interfacial reconfiguration. In LED cooling, the FPCC lowers the device temperature by up to 6.5 °C relative to a commercial thermal pad. These results establish phase-transition-driven thermomechanical regulation as a route to improving and stabilizing low-preload thermal interfaces through the coupled effects of compliance, expansion-generated loading, and interfacial reconfiguration.

title: Sulfur Locking and Chlorination Synergistically Enable Efficient Charge Transport and Low Nonradiative Energy Loss in Organic Solar Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Achieving efficient charge transport while maintaining low nonradiative energy loss remains a key challenge in the molecular design of small‐molecule acceptors (SMAs) for organic solar cells (OSCs). Herein, we report a stepwise molecular engineering strategy based on sulfur locking and chlorination to regulate intermolecular packing and excited‐state properties simultaneously. Sulfur locking modifies molecular conformation and intermolecular packing, leading to enhanced exciton diffusion and charge transport. Subsequent chlorination further strengthens intermolecular interactions through additional Cl···S contacts, resulting in tighter π–π stacking and improved crystalline ordering. Binary OSCs based on D18:Qx2Ph‐SCl achieve an efficiency of 20.0% with a high open‐circuit voltage ( V OC ) of 0.951 V, while maintaining a low nonradiative energy loss of ∼0.19 eV. Owing to its intrinsically lower reorganization energy and weaker electron–phonon coupling than L8‐BO, Qx2Ph‐SCl further serves as an effective third component in ternary OSCs, reducing nonradiative recombination and increasing the V OC . As a result, the ternary device delivers an efficiency of 21.3%. This work demonstrates that stepwise sulfur locking and chlorination provide an effective molecular design strategy for simultaneously optimizing charge transport and voltage loss in high‐performance OSCs.

title: Synergy between UiO-66-NH2 and a Hierarchical Aluminum Reservoir for Durable, Self-Replenishing Dry Lubrication
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Friction and wear limit the reliability and energy efficiency of mechanical systems, motivating solid lubricants for conditions where liquid lubricants fail. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are attractive owing to their tunable structures and ability to form protective tribofilms, but their low-yield synthesis demands strategies that maximize performance at minimal loading. Herein, we developed a synergistic dry-lubrication strategy in which a hierarchical structure (HS) acts as an integrated reservoir for UiO-66-NH2. Drop-cast MOF particles were anchored within the interconnected concavities of an etched aluminum (Al 5052) substrate bearing a micro/nano hierarchical surface. The anchored UiO-66-NH2 was continuously supplied to the contact interface as a rolling third body, infilling worn regions. Post-test SEM–EDS detected Zr across the wear track, suggesting that the MOF was compacted into a protective MOF-derived layer. The amino-functionalized UiO-66-NH2 showed slightly better wear resistance than carboxyl-functionalized UiO-66-(COOH)2, and performance was further optimized by tuning the MOF concentration (7 mg/mL) and HCl etching time (2 min). Using only 0.56 mg/cm2 of MOF, the surface reduced wear-track width and maximum wear depth by 46.6% and 62.6%, respectively, relative to bare Al sliding against a stainless-steel pin under 1 N. The friction reduction was mainly provided by the HS, whereas UiO-66-NH2 primarily suppressed wear. This durable, self-replenishing approach offers a scalable route to practical MOF-based tribological surfaces.

title: Meta-state electrolytes with quasi-ordered clusters for stable lithium metal batteries
abstract: Ionic aggregation state in liquid electrolytes is generally constrained by the salt solubility limit of the solvent matrix, restricting the accessible coordination structures and limiting opportunities for electrolyte engineering. Here, we report a class of meta-state electrolytes (MSEs) that transcend this conventional solubility limit and access an atypical aggregation regime. Enabled by external-field regulation coupled with nonequilibrium kinetic access, the MSE reshapes the Li⁺ coordination landscape and stabilizes a previously inaccessible meta-state domain beyond the threshold region of the ternary phase diagram. Within this regime, the MSE remains macroscopically homogeneous while forming large anion-rich clusters with local coordination environments resembling those of solid lithium salt, yielding an inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) with high mechanical robustness and fast Li+ transport. Accordingly, the MSE effectively suppresses interfacial parasitic reactions, enabling Cu||LiNi0.5Co0.2Mn0.3O2 pouch cells to retain 70% of their capacity after 136 cycles at 45°C. Our study establishes external-field regulation of the Li+ coordination environment as a new design principle for advanced electrolytes, with broad implications for solid/liquid interfacial chemistry.

title: Miniaturization coincides with anatomical novelties during lissamphibian origins
abstract: Evolutionary miniaturization is often accompanied by phenotypic rearrangement, and may play an important role in occupying new adaptive zones. This process has hypothesised relevance to the origin of lissamphibians, which include the smallest living tetrapods. We test this by quantifying patterns of evolution of body size and other traits, using a dataset of 577 fossil and extant members of the lissamphibian total-group. We find that initial body size reduction occurred on the direct stem lineage leading to Lissamphibia and further miniaturization occurred in the crown group, giving rise to the down-shifted size distribution of living species. This coincides with rearrangements of skull morphology and the diversification of body shapes, indicating invasion of a fundamentally distinct adaptive zone. Our finding provides a compelling case of the potential contribution of miniaturization to ecological innovation at a macroevolutionary scale, facilitating the diversification and persistence of lissamphibians through ∼300 million years of evolutionary time.

title: Observation of a magneto-nonlinear Hall effect in an altermagnet candidate
abstract: Nonlinear Hall effects have emerged as defining probes of quantum geometry. Here we observe a Hall response that is nonlinear in the magnetic field rather than the electric field, in Mn5Si3 thin films, an altermagnet candidate, in the canonical Hall geometry: a high-field Hall conductivity component that grows quadratically with an out-of-plane field. Opposite-sign Berry curvatures associated with opposite-spin bands nearly cancel at low fields, but Zeeman band shifts at high fields lift this cancellation and generate increasing net total Berry curvature. This magnetic-field-tuned Berry-curvature imbalance can generally produce a nonlinear Hall conductivity, and the observed quadratic dependence in Mn5Si3 is consistent with chiral next-nearest-neighbor hopping involving magnetic exchange and Haldane-like flux phases. Moreover, reversal of magnetic order under opposite fields reverses the hopping chirality, making this quadratic contribution odd in field. Beyond fundamental advances, the nonlinear response remains unsaturated up to 57 T, suggesting possible opportunities for high-field Hall sensing.

title: Comparative PECS and LPBF Processing of Bi0.5Sb1.5Te3: Microstructure, Texture, and Thermoelectric Performance
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is emerging as a promising manufacturing route for next-generation thermoelectric generators, offering unprecedented freedom in the fabrication of complex device geometries. However, the rapid melting and solidification inherent to LPBF produce microstructures fundamentally different from those of conventional consolidation techniques, and how these processing-induced features affect thermoelectric performance remains poorly understood. In this work, LPBF-produced p-type Bi0.5Sb1.5Te3 was compared with materials fabricated by pulsed electric current sintering (PECS), which served as a reference processing route providing a higher degree of crystallographic texture. The comparison enabled identification of the microstructural characteristics governing electrical and thermal transport. In particular, the investigated materials exhibited a wide range of preferred orientation (Lotgering factor F ≈ 0.02–0.20), while maintaining comparable Seebeck coefficients (∼160–175 μV K–1). In contrast, electrical conductivity (720–2200 S cm–1 at 300 K), thermal conductivity (0.9–1.5 W m–1 K–1), and consequently the thermoelectric figure of merit varied strongly with the processing route and crystallographic orientation. PECS samples with moderate preferred orientation reached ZT ≈ 1.1, while LPBF specimens exhibited ZT ≈ 0.4–0.5. The lower LPBF performance reflects weaker texture and processing-induced defects, partly related to nonideal powder morphology and feeding conditions. Additionally, numerical modeling (FEM) was performed to evaluate energy conversion efficiency, demonstrating higher output power and overall efficiency for the PECS samples compared to the LPBF ones. The comparative analysis demonstrates that crystallographic texture and microstructural integrity are key factors affecting thermoelectric performance and identifies processing-related limitations under the LPBF conditions investigated in this study.

title: Printed Flexible and Recyclable Heterojunction for Water Cleanup
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract To address the issues of easy agglomeration, difficult recovery, and poor engineering applicability faced by traditional powdered photocatalysts in water treatment, this study proposes a laser-induced transient thermal modulation electrohydrodynamic jet (LTMJ) printing strategy, enabling the direct immobilization of pre-synthesized g-C3N4/BiOI heterojunction particles on flexible quartz fiber cloth in a single printing step, thereby fabricating a high-performance and recyclable photocatalytic platform. By virtue of the real-time coupling between the laser field and the electrohydrodynamic jet printing process, a controllable transient non-equilibrium thermal environment is established in the flying droplet region. The explosive evaporation triggered by laser-droplet energy coupling effectively suppresses the secondary agglomeration of particles and regulates the deposition and interparticle assembly of the pre-synthesized heterojunction particles. Without damaging the crystalline phase and heterojunction structure of the materials, this method simultaneously achieves particle size refinement and enhancement of the uniformity and compactness of the deposited layer. Under visible light irradiation, this flexible platform exhibits excellent degradation activity and cyclic stability toward various organic dyes, while it is easy to recover and regenerate. This study not only provides a new method for the precise fabrication of flexible and recyclable photocatalytic devices, but also offers novel insights into the multi-physics field coupling-regulated assembly and functionalization of micro-nanostructures.

title: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    When anthropogenic CO
                    2
                    emissions cease, global temperature does not stabilize immediately. The resulting global temperature change, the zero emissions commitment, is central to carbon budget assessments and understanding reversibility of global warming, yet its dependence on prior warming levels remains unclear. Here we show, using zero-emission simulations with the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.2) across global warming levels of 1.5–5 K, that the zero emissions commitment stays near zero up to 2 K but becomes positive at higher warming levels, reaching 0.4–0.6 K after ~ 150 years. This dependence indicates that stabilizing or reversing warming becomes progressively more difficult as peak temperature rises. We identify the mechanism behind this behaviour: stronger warming from higher radiative disequilibrium and weakening carbon sinks, driven by saturated land carbon uptake and the reduced radiative impact of CO
                    2
                    drawdown at higher background CO
                    2
                    concentrations. Higher peak warming therefore commits the planet to additional warming, limiting temperature-overshoot reversibility.

title: Reconfiguring Quinone Cathodes via Transition Metal Coordination for Advanced Calcium Batteries
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Calcium-ion batteries (CIBs) are promising for next-generation energy storage. However, their development is hindered by the lack of high-performance cathode materials. Organic carbonyl compounds possess structural flexibility and redox activity, yet their overall energy density remains fundamentally constrained. Here, we report a molecular engineering strategy to prepare metal (Cu and Ni)-coordinated quinone cathodes. The incorporation of transition-metal centers reconfigures the conjugated molecular framework, simultaneously enhancing reversible capacity and operating voltage. The optimized cathodes deliver reversible capacities of up to 203 mAh g–1 at an average voltage of ∼3.1 V vs Ca2+/Ca, corresponding to an energy density exceeding 600 Wh kg–1. Mechanistic investigations based on in situ characterizations and theoretical calculations reveal a bipolar charge-storage mechanism involving Ca2+ coordination with the carbonyl and imine sites during discharge and TFSI– storage at high charging potentials. This metal-coordination strategy provides a promising strategy for developing high-energy multivalent battery systems.

title: Microscopic Intricacies of Self-Healing in Halide Perovskite–Charge-Transport-Layer Heterostructures
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The operational stability of halide perovskite photovoltaics is critically limited by progressive defect generation and nonradiative losses. Self-healing of defects offers a promising route to sustained performance, yet the coupled microscopic processes underlying it remain poorly understood, particularly at device-relevant interfaces. Here, we elucidate self-healing and defect evolution in photodamaged triple-cation mixed-halide (TCMH) perovskite films and their device-relevant charge-transport-layer (CTL) heterostructures. Using correlation clustering imaging (CLIM), our recently developed microscopic functional imaging tool, we map spatiotemporal photoluminescence heterogeneity to track defect dynamics. Each CTL distinctly modulates local trap activity, healing kinetics, and spectral redistribution in the TCMH layer, and the heterostructures exhibit faster optical recovery than pristine films, beneficial for device resilience. Healing follows biphasic kinetics, with fast electronic relaxation over minutes to tens of minutes and slower ionic redistribution and lattice relaxation over hours. Although quantitative device stability improvements are not established here, these microscopic insights into dynamic evolution of defects and ion redistribution at interfaces provide a framework for rationally designing stable perovskite optoelectronics.

title: Nanoscale Thermal Imaging of Dislocation‐Mediated Heat Transport
abstract: ABSTRACT Dislocations are widely used to tailor lattice thermal conductivity in semiconductors and thermoelectrics, yet the local thermal resistance of individual buried dislocations and their spatial extent remain experimentally unresolved. Here, operando scanning transmission electron microscopy–electron energy‐loss spectroscopy thermometry, atomic‐resolution imaging, vibrational spectroscopy, and nonequilibrium molecular dynamics are combined to map heat transport across a dislocation array within a 5°SrTiO 3 low‐angle grain boundary. The effective thermal conductance of the dislocation array is estimated to be ∼35.4 MW m − 2 K − 1 using the bulk reference conductivity, corresponding to a Kapitza length of ∼339 nm. Nanoscale temperature maps reveal a spatially heterogeneous resistance landscape: reconstructed dislocation cores act as sharp thermal bottlenecks over ∼2.14–5.17 nm, with steeper local temperature gradients than inter‐core regions, whereas inter‐core regions show weaker but more extended modulation over ∼8.34–11.57 nm. Correlative structural and vibrational analyses show that Ti─O bond distortion, Ti valence change, P4 optical‐phonon blueshift, and reduced local–bulk phonon density‐of‐states overlap create a core‐specific vibrational environment. These results uncover the underlying mechanism whereby atomic‐scale core reconstruction generates nanoscale localized thermal resistance, and offer quantitative descriptors for defect‐structure‐guided thermal design.

title: Scalable Gigapascal Strength Bamboo Veneers via Nanocellulose Reinforcement
abstract: ABSTRACT Carbon neutrality demands materials that deliver both performance and low environmental impact. Carbon fiber and glass fiber rely on fossil feedstocks and energy‐intensive processing, while nature bamboo the ecological marvel is limited by inefficient load transfer within their heterogeneous cell walls. Here we show that this limitation can be overcome by reprogramming the bamboo cell wall through supramolecular nano‐reinforcement. Cellulose nanocrystals infiltrate the cell wall and promote the reorganization of the interfacial hydrogen‐bonding network within the aligned cellulose framework converting structural discontinuities into a continuous load‐bearing scaffold. This enhances interfibrillar stress transfer and homogenizes mechanical response across scales. The resulting material achieves a tensile strength of 0.98 GPa and a Young's modulus of 52.7 GPa, with specific strength rivaling many synthetic fiber materials. These gains are achieved with up to two orders of magnitude lower carbon intensity than that of carbon fiber. This work demonstrates a scalable route to transform abundant biomass into high‐performance structural materials, decoupling mechanical performance from carbon intensity.

title: Semi-Embedded Liquid Metal Nanoparticles on Co-Electrospun Nanofibers for Scalable and High-Sensitivity Flexible Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering Platform
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Flexible surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) substrates are essential for conformal on-site molecular detection, yet typically face a trade-off between sensitivity, uniformity, and mechanical robustness. In this work, we report a high-performance flexible SERS featuring liquid metal nanoparticles spatially confined within electrospun polyimide nanofibers. Via co-electrospinning, we engineered a unique “semi-embedded” structure where liquid metal nanoparticles are partially exposed on fiber surfaces. The optimized substrate achieves an ultralow detection limit (LOD) of 10–8 M for Rhodamine 6G with outstanding signal uniformity and excellent mechanical durability (72.5% signal retention after 500 bending cycles), compared to existing flexible platforms. Furthermore, the platform enables sensitive and differentiated SERS detection of thiol-containing molecules, with preferential trace detection of 4-aminothiophenol (LOD 10–9 M). Its practical utility is further demonstrated by the simultaneous monitoring of mixed acetamiprid and thiram residues in apple juice. Finite-element simulations suggest that the superior SERS enhancement under near‑infrared excitation is largely consistent with synergistic electromagnetic coupling between the sputtered Au nanoparticles and the highly conductive liquid metal cores, with possible additional chemical enhancement from the oxide-rich surface. This study presents a cost-effective and scalable strategy for fabricating high-performance SERS substrates while offering critical insights into the synergistic coupling between liquid metals and conventional plasmonic materials.

title: Comprehensively Unveiling the Dual Antifungal and Antibacterial Activity of Ultra-small Pt Nanoclusters through Membrane Impairment Induced by Oxidative Stress
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and viruses, can invade the human body, disrupt normal physiological functions, and trigger a variety of infectious diseases, currently posing a significant global health issue. Silver (Ag), gold (Au), and titanium dioxide (TiO2) nanomaterials have already demonstrated exciting antimicrobial properties and promising therapeutic applications. However, the antibacterial performance of Pt nanomaterials, especially nanoclusters (NCs, <2 nm), has rarely been investigated. In this study, Pt NCs with an ultra-small size of 1.5 ± 0.5 nm were produced by a reduction method, and their structure presents a composite of fine atomic clusters. A series of bacteriostatic experiments proved that the sterilizing rates of Gram-negative bacteria Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Gram-positive bacteria Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) are 98.02 and 99.99%, respectively. In addition, the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) of Pt NCs against Fusarium solani (F. solani) were determined to be as low as 0.8 and 1.7 μg/mL, and these Pt NCs exhibited fungicidal activity. The antibacterial and antifungal mechanisms were elucidated, showing that the oxidative stress generated via the excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) induced by Pt NCs triggers the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation (LPO), consequently causing the structural degradation and functional impairment of membranes, ultimately resulting in the cytoplasmic contents leaking and bacterial/fungal death. Astonishingly, the wound healing rate for methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) infections was 98.90% at 10 days post treatment by Pt NCs, indicating significantly higher efficacy than that of the conventional broad-spectrum antibacterial fluoroquinolone drug ofloxacin. Furthermore, the antimicrobial gauze fabricated using these Pt NCs exhibited at least 99.75% inhibition of both E. coli and S. aureus within 24 h, suggesting their promising application prospects as a novel and safer antibacterial and antifungal agent.

title: Rational Design of Plasmonic Nanoarrays for Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering Applications
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Plasmonic nanoarrays have emerged as attractive platforms for surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS), offering systematic control over geometry, optical response, and interfacial properties. This review focuses on the rational design and template-assisted fabrication of plasmonic nanoarrays for SERS. We first summarize the electromagnetic and chemical enhancement mechanisms and discuss design considerations specific to these nanoarrays, including particle geometry, substrate effects, and collective plasmonic coupling. We then review representative fabrication strategies based on nanosphere and anodic aluminum oxide templates, highlighting how template geometry and deposition conditions, material composition, and interfacial engineering enable the construction of coupled, anisotropic, multicomponent, and flexible nanoarrays. Finally, we discuss their applications in analytical SERS and mechanistic studies of interfacial processes. Particular attention is given to hotspot engineering, molecular accessibility and selectivity, and the use of structurally defined nanoarrays to probe charge transfer, hot-carrier processes, and plasmon-mediated reactions.

title: Fabrication of MoS2 Nanopores via Dielectric Breakdown for Single-Molecule Sensing Applications
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract This study focuses on the controllable fabrication of monolayer molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) nanopores based on dielectric breakdown and their application in single-molecule sensing. To address the poor pore-size controllability and limited reproducibility commonly encountered in the fabrication of sub-5 nm transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) nanopores, the nanopore formation processes under voltage-stepping and current-stepping modes were systematically investigated. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with the voltage-stepping mode, the current-stepping mode exhibits a more gradual breakdown transition. Although the average breakdown times of the two modes are comparable, the nanopores fabricated by current stepping are confined to a narrower sub-5 nm range, whereas voltage stepping produces a broader distribution. Consequently, precise and controllable fabrication of sub-5 nm TMD nanopores was achieved. The fabricated MoS2 nanopore sensor was further employed for single-molecule detection of oligonucleotide (Oligo) DNA, where distinct ionic current blockade events were successfully recorded. Combined with COMSOL Multiphysics simulations, three representative translocation behaviors were identified and elucidated. This work provides systematic experimental and theoretical insights into the high-precision fabrication of TMD nanopores and their potential applications in biosensing.

title: Vertical Graphene/Violet-Phosphorus/Graphene Photodetectors for Wavelength-Programmed Optical Signal Encoding
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract As an emerging two-dimensional van der Waals material, violet phosphorus is particularly notable for its ambient stability, moderate bandgap, and strong light absorption, making it an excellent candidate for photodetection applications. However, conventional lateral-channel devices based on violet phosphorus typically suffer from severe carrier recombination losses over extended transport distances. Here, we demonstrate a high-performance vertical-channel photodetector based on a graphene/violet phosphorus/graphene (Gr/VP/Gr) van der Waals heterostructure. By shortening the carrier transport path, the vertical architecture enables efficient carrier collection and a high photoconductive gain. Under 532 nm illumination, the device achieves a responsivity of 1.7 × 104 A/W, a specific detectivity of 2.1 × 1013 Jones, and an external quantum efficiency of approximately 3.9 × 106%; its photoresponse spans 450–1050 nm. A transport-scaling analysis comparing vertical and lateral geometries indicates that the vertical structure reduces the carrier drift transit time to the picosecond scale, providing a quantitative rationale for the large effective gain. The device also exhibits wavelength-dependent transient dynamics, with a relatively fast response at 450 nm and a persistent response at 800 nm. These distinct temporal signatures enable a proof-of-concept demonstration of wavelength-programmed optical signal encoding. The outstanding optoelectronic performance of Gr/VP/Gr vertical heterostructures establishes them as an innovative and versatile platform for next-generation broadband photodetection and secure optical data transmission systems with enhanced quantum efficiency and spectral adaptability.

title: Overcoming B16F10 Melanoma by Local Co-Delivering Chemotherapeutics and Anti-Angiogenic Agents Using Injectable Thermoresponsive Polypeptide Hydrogels
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, along with the vascular barrier within B16F10 melanoma, frequently compromises the therapeutic outcomes of antitumor immunotherapy. Hydrogels, possessing three-dimensional network structures, provide a platform for localized drug delivery. Herein, we reported a thermoresponsive polypeptide hydrogel co-loaded with mitoxantrone (MTX) and the angiogenesis inhibitor nintedanib (NE), combined with immune checkpoint blockade therapy, to address these challenges. Results demonstrated that the release of MTX induced immunogenic cell death of tumor cells and released tumor-associated antigens, while the release of NE inhibited angiogenesis, promoted drug permeation and immune cell infiltration, enhanced therapeutic efficacy, and suppressed tumor proliferation and metastasis. In a melanoma-bearing mouse model, the combination of intratumoral injection of MTX/NE-loaded hydrogel with intravenous injection of anti-PD-1 elicited a strong systemic anti-tumor immune response, successfully inhibiting tumor growth and metastasis, while prolonging animal survival. Overall, this study established a hydrogel drug delivery strategy to overcome B16F10 melanoma, demonstrating strong potential in clinical cancer therapy.

title: Spin-Resolved Topology of Mem-Emitter Response
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract We develop a general framework for spin-resolved mem-emitters and illustrate it unequivocally using a monolayer MoSe2/clinochlore optoelectronic device. In mem-emitters, both the intensity and energy of light emission encode the history of external driving through slowly evolving internal state variables. When spin is included as an active degree of freedom, voltage-controlled memory dynamics give rise to spin-resolved hysteresis revealed through the degree of circular polarization under magnetic fields. Using polarization-resolved magneto-photoluminescence, we observe pronounced hysteresis in excitonic and trionic emission, whose loop topology depends on magnetic field and circular polarization. A minimal spin-resolved model shows that these features are generically governed by a polarity-dependent tuning of the effective Landé g-factor, with its voltage slope uniquely determining the orientation of the degree-of-circular-polarization loops. First-principles calculations suggest that interface-induced symmetry breaking provides a microscopic route to such bias-dependent spin responses, highlighting the broad relevance of spin-resolved memory effects in optoelectronic emitters.

title: Vanillin-Based Covalent Adaptable Networks with Ultralow Graphene Content for Enhanced Mechanical Robustness, Photothermal Self-Healing, and Corrosion Protection
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Designing partially bio-based covalent adaptable networks that combine mechanical robustness with thermally or optically triggered healing and reprocessability remains challenging because network reinforcement typically reduces dynamic chain mobility. Herein, we report a vanillin-derived imine-based network reinforced by silane-functionalized graphene oxide nanosheets covalently grafted at an ultralow loading of 0.5 wt %. The covalent anchoring of graphene oxide at the network interface raises the apparent activation energy of stress relaxation from 45.0 to 73.7 kJ mol–1 while preserving Arrhenius-type temperature dependence, consistent with increased network constraint rather than enhanced intrinsic exchange kinetics. The composite retains 84.1% of its tensile strength after three hot-press reprocessing cycles. Under near-infrared irradiation, the grafted graphene oxide enables photothermal heating that locally compensates for the reduced intrinsic chain mobility, allowing surface scratches to heal within 5 min. As a protective coating, the composite maintains an impedance modulus above 109 Ω cm2 after 130 d of saline immersion, with the improved barrier performance attributed to combined effects of tortuous diffusion pathways and reduced network free volume. These results demonstrate that an ultralow fraction of covalently grafted nanofiller can simultaneously introduce mechanical reinforcement, photothermal responsiveness, and prolonged barrier function without eliminating the dynamic character of the network.

title: Proton Irradiation Reconfigures Temperature-Dependent Emissive Heterogeneity in Wide-Bandgap All-Inorganic CsPbI2Br Perovskite Solar Cells
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Wide-bandgap metal-halide perovskites are attractive for space power due to their high open-circuit voltages and compatibility with tandem device architectures, but their response to orbital stressors remains under-explored. Here, we show that 1.86 eV all-inorganic CsPbI2Br perovskite solar cells (PSCs) develop an emissive heterogeneity when cooled to 193 K (–80 °C), marked by the emergence of distinctly bright, blue-shifted emission centers near 1.89 eV. This low-temperature blue shift is accompanied by an increased open-circuit voltage but reduced charge extraction, as revealed by operando current–voltage measurements. As the operating temperature increases to 373 K (+100 °C), the spatial emissive contrast becomes less pronounced and emission is quenched, yielding a comparatively more spatially uniform emission landscape and improved charge extraction. Irradiation of these n-i-p PSCs with 1.0 MeV protons at a fluence of 5 × 1013 cm–2 reconfigures the emissive heterogeneity, with enhanced spatial contrast at 193 K including linewidth narrowing of certain emissive components and persistent emissive features at warmer temperatures. These results suggest that proton irradiation modifies the emissive landscape in ways not fully captured by room-temperature device metrics alone. More broadly, we demonstrate that the apparent radiation tolerance of wide-bandgap PSCs at room temperature can mask the underlying heterogeneity that becomes significantly more visible under space-relevant thermal extremes.

title: Body-Coupled Organic Electrochemical Transistors for Imperceptible Skin Bioelectronics
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The efficient ion-to-electron transduction mechanism makes organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) stand out for physiological sensing. Usually, OECT operations require saline solutions or hydrogels to function as the electrolytes; however, the wet electrolytes may compromise wear comfort and device stability for human-integrated applications. In this work, we propose a body-coupled OECT (b-OECT) device mechanism, where the skin and subcutaneous tissues act as natural electrolyte for the device operation. In the b-OECT, the organic semiconducting channel forms intimate and substrate-free contact with skins, enabling biofluid-derived ionic pathways to directly mediate gate–channel coupling and electrochemical modulation. The devices exhibit body-coupled transistor characteristics, skin-coupled operation, and ion-mediated neuromorphic-like conductance modulation. Without needing external supplied electrolytes, the b-OECT offers breathable and imperceptible body integration, where biological tissue directly participates in electrochemical signal transduction, opening potentials for skin-integrated bioelectronics and body-coupled neuromorphic biointerfaces.

title: Dynamic Electronic Modulation of MOF-808 via Vacancy-Driven Ligand-to-Metal Charge Transfer for Self-amplifying Photocatalysis
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The mechanistic insight into the relationship between pollutant adsorption and the corresponding photocatalytic response remains a critical yet elusive facet of heterogeneous catalysis. Here, we unravel the multiplicity of adsorption pathways governing norfloxacin (NOR) uptake on oxygen- and organic-vacancy-engineered MOF-808 (MOF-808-OVs) and demonstrate that these interfacial interactions actively reconfigure the framework’s electronic landscape through a vacancy-driven ligand-to-metal charge transfer (v-LMCT) process. While Lewis acid–base pairing and electrostatic forces at the Zr–O clusters constitute the primary binding determinants, π–π stacking and hydrophobic contacts serve as auxiliary contributions. Crucially, combined partial density of states (PDOS) analysis reveals that the resultant MOF-808–pollutant adduct enables a v-LMCT pathway, wherein electron injection from NOR into the O 2p orbitals of the Zr–O nodes not only reinforces adsorbate retention but also primes a rapid electron shuttling cascade from the inorganic clusters to dissolved O2 in aqueous media. This synergistic charge-transfer regime substantially amplifies reactive oxygen species generation, boosting •OH and 1O2 production by factors of 2.2 and 6.0, respectively, relative to pristine MOF-808 in the absence of NOR. Thus, these findings establish a mechanistic paradigm wherein adsorption serves as an electronic tuning lever, engendering a self-amplifying photocatalytic cycle. This work provides a foundational strategy for the rational design of next-generation photocatalysts predicated on adsorption-driven electronic modulation.

title: Enhanced Proton Irradiation Resistance of Mo/Si EUV Multilayers with Ultrathin B4C Barriers
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Proton-induced structural degradation seriously threatens the long-term reliability of Mo/Si multilayers for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) astronomical observations, which calls for in-depth mechanistic analysis and anti-irradiation optimization schemes. In this work, 40 keV proton irradiation with fluences up to 5 × 1016 p/cm2 was performed on Mo/Si and Mo/B4C/Si/B4C multilayers to characterize the fluence-dependent structural evolution of Mo/Si multilayers and clarify how the interlayers formed from decomposed B4C enhance proton irradiation tolerance. Based on the experimental characterizations, the Mo/Si multilayer exhibited pronounced self-limiting period compaction and asymmetric interface broadening with increasing proton fluence. In contrast, merely sub-angstrom period expansion occurred in the Mo/B4C/Si/B4C multilayer under the maximum fluence exposure. Combined experimental characterizations and Monte Carlo simulations reveal that Si-dominated atomic interdiffusion drives the formation of dense MoSi2 interlayers and subsequent period compaction. Moreover, Si atoms preferentially diffuse forward to Si-on-Mo interfaces, resulting in asymmetric interface broadening. Meanwhile, the progressively thickened MoSi2 interlayers suppress further Si migration and lead to the self-limiting degradation behavior. For the Mo/B4C/Si/B4C multilayer, the reaction between the ultrathin B4C layers and adjacent Mo and Si layers produces boride- and carbide-containing interlayers. Compared with MoSi2 interlayers, these interlayers suppress proton-induced Si diffusion by a factor of about 3.0, which arises from their higher atomic density and larger screened Coulomb scattering cross section. These findings demonstrate that B4C insertion effectively mitigates proton-induced interdiffusion and structural degradation, offering a reliable route to improve the proton irradiation resistance of Mo/Si EUV multilayer mirrors for the forthcoming Xihe-2 mission.

title: Enzyme−Antibiotic Liquid Crystalline Nanoparticles for Enhanced Antibiofilm Activity, Bacterial Clearance, and Accelerated Healing of Infected Wounds
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Biofilm-associated wound infections remain difficult to treat because bacteria are protected within extracellular polymeric matrices that restrict antibiotic penetration, promote antimicrobial tolerance, and delay tissue repair. Here, we developed liquid crystalline nanoparticles (LCNPs) for topical coformulation of gentamicin (GEN) and recombinant human DNase I (rhDNase), combining aminoglycoside therapy with an eDNA-targeting enzyme. GEN + rhDNase-LCNPs were successfully formulated as nanoscale particles with low polydispersity, high encapsulation efficiency, and formulation-dependent in vitro release behavior. LCNP formulation preserved GEN antibacterial activity against planktonic Escherichia coli Xen14 and reduced the MBIC against established biofilms by approximately 4-fold. In a minimum biofilm eradication concentration (MBEC) model, GEN + rhDNase-LCNPs achieved the greatest reduction in biofilm-associated viable bacteria, producing an approximately 6-log reduction compared with untreated biofilm controls and supporting the benefit of combining antibiotic delivery with rhDNase. Notably, GEN + rhDNase-LCNPs markedly suppressed bacterial burden and reduced recoverable bacteria at day 9 to near the limit of detection in a bioluminescent E. coli Xen14 biofilm-associated excisional wound infection mouse model. This antibacterial effect translated into accelerated macroscopic wound closure and improved histological repair, including an approximately 80% reduction in wound gape compared with infected controls. Masson’s trichrome staining further confirmed enhanced tissue remodeling, with the collagen-positive wound area increasing to approximately 88% following GEN + rhDNase-LCNP treatment, compared with approximately 21% in infected controls. In conclusion, LCNP-mediated codelivery of GEN and rhDNase improved bacterial clearance, re-epithelialization, and collagen deposition, supporting this platform as a promising topical antibiofilm strategy for infected wounds.

title: Co-Assembled MOF@SiO2 Nanostructures for Superhydrophobic and Electrically Insulating Radiative Cooling Coatings
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Passive radiative cooling (PRC) technology, characterized by zero-energy cooling capability, has shown great promise for thermal management of high-voltage electrical equipment. However, such application scenarios impose stringent multifunctional requirements on PRC coatings, including superhydrophobicity to resist surface contamination, as well as high electrical insulation strength to prevent surface flashover. Here, we report a co-assembly strategy for constructing multifunctional PRC coatings through the in situ integration of a metal-organic framework (MOF) with a silica precursor. The appropriately tailored bandgap (Eg = 4.25 eV) of the MOF, slightly exceeding the upper photon-energy bound of the measured solar band (4.13 eV), enables suppressed solar absorption while affording a strong mid-infrared emissivity. Meanwhile, the high-Eg SiO2 shell effectively passivates intrinsic insulation defects and the high surface energy associated with MOFs, thereby enhancing both dielectric reliability and superhydrophobicity. Consequently, the optimized PRC coating delivered a temperature drop of 10.6 ± 0.5 °C during outdoor testing, together with robust superhydrophobicity (153.7°) and high wet flashover strength (15.6 kV/cm). This work advances PRC coatings beyond conventional thermal regulation by integrating radiative cooling, surface self-cleaning, and electrical insulation into a unified material platform, opening new opportunities for passive thermal management of high-voltage electrical equipment.

title: Analysis of the Coercivity Mechanism of High-Performance Nd-Fe-B Magnets Prepared by Synergistic Diffusion
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The grain boundary diffusion process is an important approach for preparing high-performance Nd-Fe-B magnets. In this study, Nd-Fe-B diffusion magnets with both high remanence and high coercivity were prepared via a two-step synergistic diffusion process. The process combined Pr70Ga30 pre-diffusion with subsequent DyH3 diffusion. Compared with DyH3 diffusion alone, this two-step synergistic diffusion strategy increased the coercivity increment from 3.30 to 3.84 kOe while maintaining a remanence of 15.03 kG. Microstructural and elemental analyses showed that Pr70Ga30 pre-diffusion modified the grain-boundary phase and promoted Dy diffusion to greater depths. The modified grain boundaries facilitated the formation of continuous (Dy, RE)2Fe14B shells around the main-phase grains. These shells increased the local magnetocrystalline anisotropy and strengthened the grain edges against reverse-domain nucleation. Micromagnetic simulations indicated that a complete core-shell structure increased the demagnetization nucleation field at grain edges, thereby suppressing magnetic domain reversal. This study establishes a direct relationship between grain-boundary modification, shell continuity, and coercivity enhancement in Nd-Fe-B magnets.

title: Composite Cathodes for Oxide-Based Solid-State Batteries: Processing, Interfacial Mechanisms, and Performance Engineering
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Composite cathodes are a key component in oxide-based solid-state batteries (SSBs), enabling electrochemical activity through the integration of cathode active materials, solid electrolytes, and conductive additives within a single composite architecture. However, their performance is strongly influenced by complex interfacial phenomena and chemo-mechanical effects arising from heterogeneous solid−solid contacts, which often result in high interfacial resistance, limited percolation of ionic and electronic pathways, and progressive degradation during processing and cycling. This review aims to clarify how composite cathode designs govern the performance of oxide-based SSBs, focusing on the interplay between material selection, fabrication routes (wet and dry processes), interfacial structure evolution, and transport efficiency. Emphasis is placed on critical challenges such as co-sintering-induced interfacial degradation, space−charge layer formation, poor contact, and an imbalance between ionic and electronic transport, as well as on strategies developed to address these issues, including buffer layers, co-sintering additives, and microstructural engineering. Advanced characterization techniques are also discussed for probing buried interfaces and correlating structure with performance. Finally, we identify critical gaps in current understanding and outline prospective research pathways aimed at formulating robust design guidelines for oxide-based composite cathodes with enhanced mechanical integrity and electrochemical stability, ultimately advancing high-performance oxide-based SSBs.

title: Piezoelectric-Excitation-Enabled Saturated-Charge Regulation for Active Noncontact Triboelectric Sensing
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Surface charges on triboelectric materials inherently exist in a nonsaturated, dynamically decaying state. Consequently, passive noncontact inductive sensing produces signals with pronounced amplitude fluctuations and baseline drift. To address these limitations, we introduce an active excitation strategy based on a piezoelectric layer: periodic mechanical actuation induces reversible polarization, thereby modulating the local electric field to enable real-time replenishment and spatial redistribution of surface charges on the triboelectric layer. This mechanism markedly enhances both signal amplitude and long-term stability. Furthermore, intrinsic material properties, including relative permittivity, surface resistivity, thickness, and surface charge retention capacity, introduce systematic variations in coupling capacitance, induced charge transfer pathways, and charge relaxation dynamics across different target materials in noncontact configurations. By employing frequency-swept excitation, static dielectric and charge-related differences among materials are transduced into distinctive dynamic frequency-response signatures, substantially improving multimaterial classification accuracy. Critically, this approach retains the key advantages of noncontact operation and zero mechanical wear, while effectively reducing surface contamination and introducing active signal conditioning, thereby distinguishing it from conventional contact-mode triboelectric classification and passive noncontact sensing paradigms. Finally, by fusing time-domain, frequency-domain, and time-frequency features within a decision tree-based classification framework, the system achieves >95% recognition accuracy across diverse material classes, demonstrating a scalable, robust, and actively enhanced triboelectric sensing platform suitable for online material sorting, thin-film quality inspection, and robotic tactile perception.

title: Nonlinear Curved Metasurfaces for Enhanced Thyroid Magnetic Resonance Imaging
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Metasurfaces offer a promising approach to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Thyroid MRI suffers from insufficient SNR due to the anatomical irregularity of the neck and poor coil-to-tissue proximity, which fails to meet the demands of preoperative tumor diagnosis. This work introduces a nonlinear, curved metasurface tailored to address these limitations through a nonlinear mode control scheme based on up-frequency tuning. Unlike the previously reported down-frequency tuning scheme, here the metasurface's resonant frequency is selectively shifted to a frequency above the Larmor frequency during RF transmit via an integrated diode-inductor circuit, thereby minimizing B1+ perturbation and specific absorption rate increase. Concurrently, its conformal curved geometry focuses the enhanced field on the concave side, optimizing penetration for superficial targets. This adaptive mechanism minimally perturbs the transmit field while keeping the device fully active during signal reception. Experiments demonstrate that this thyroid imaging curved metasurface (TCM) provides an SNR enhancement by a factor of over six in the target thyroid region and an effective penetration depth of approximately 60 mm over the whole range of up-frequency inductances examined (27–100 nH), for which the two-fold gain is maintained to about 70 mm, validating its potential as a practical, wireless adjunct for high-quality thyroid MRI.

title: A Complex-Anion-Doped Ionic-Liquid Electrolyte for High-Voltage Cathodes in Lithium-Ion Batteries
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract High-voltage cathodes can increase the energy density of lithium-ion batteries, but they impose stringent requirements on electrolyte oxidation resistance and safety. Traditional carbonate-based electrolytes can undergo oxidative decomposition at high potentials, which limits their application to high-voltage cathodes. Ionic liquids (ILs) are considered to be promising candidates for the construction of high-safety and high-voltage electrolytes due to their extremely low vapor pressure, low flammability and wide electrochemical window. In this paper, a multi-anion modification strategy was introduced into the ionic liquid electrolyte to create a complex-anion-doped ionic liquid electrolyte (CAD-ILE), which modifies the local ionic environment while retaining the main spectral features of the ionic liquid. On a formulation-component basis, CAD-ILE contains 60 mol % EMIMTFSI, 37 mol % LiTFSI, and 3 mol % auxiliary salts (LiFSI, LiPF6, LiBOB, LiBF4, LiDFP, LiOTF, LiDFOB, and LiNO3; 0.375 mol % each). This formulation is associated with a thin, LiF-containing CEI on the cathode surface. The capacity retention of the CAD-ILE electrolyte is 71% after 200 cycles at 4.6 V in a LCO||Li half cell (only 32% in commercial electrolyte), and 87% after 120 cycles at 4.55 V in a LCO||graphite full cell. This work supports a simple and effective high-voltage electrolyte design strategy.

title: Flexible Artificial Neurons Based on NbO x for Robust Tactile Perception in a Wide Temperature Range
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Neuromorphic tactile sensing that emulates biological touch enables artificial systems to work with high efficiency and low energy consumption. As tactile-sensing scenarios may involve curved surfaces and different temperatures, artificial spiking afferent neurons require both flexibility and temperature robustness at the front end of artificial systems. Here, we report flexible artificial spiking neurons based on niobium oxide (NbOx) threshold-switching (TS) memristors prepared on polyimide (PI) substrates. Temperature-dependent transport analysis indicates that their temperature robustness is associated with a bulk switching pathway in the NbOx film. By integrating an oscillation circuit, the NbOx spiking afferent neurons convert analog inputs into frequency-modulated voltage spikes and retain oscillatory capability from –80 to 80 °C at a bending radius of 5 mm. Moreover, pressure sensors are coupled with the NbOx neurons to form mechanoreceptors that encode pressure as oscillation frequency. In the numerical tactile-recognition workflow, a convolutional neural network (CNN) classifies spatial frequency maps generated from the fitted pressure-to-frequency relations, achieving accuracies of 97.5% under the baseline condition and 93.2% at 80 °C at a bending radius of 5 mm. This work demonstrates that flexible NbOx neurons can serve as compact event-driven front ends for wide-temperature robotic tactile sensing.

title: Development of Novel Ridge-and-Valley Form Small-Caliber Compliant Vascular Grafts Based on a Modified Near-Field Coaxial Electrospinning Technique
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Limited attention has been paid to the macroscopic topology of small-caliber electrospinning artificial vascular grafts. Here, we fabricated an elastic vascular graft of 2 mm diameter featuring a “ridge-and-valley” macrostructure using a modified near-field coaxial electrospinning technology, which combines the near-field electrospinning direct-writing technique and coaxial electrospinning technology, employing polyurethane (PU) as the outer shell and poly(l-lactide-co-ε-caprolactone) (PLCL) as the inner core. By adjusting the PLCL/PU ratio, the viscosity of the blended solution was tuned to meet electrospinning requirements. The electrospun grafts exhibited oriented filament alignment in the ridge regions and a relatively disordered configuration in the valley regions, demonstrating significantly enhanced kinking resistance in macroscopic testing. In vitro cell experiments and in situ rat abdominal aorta transplantation models verified the graft's ability in inducing vascular smooth muscle cell (vSMC) alignment generated by oriented fiber alignment. Importantly, partial endothelial coverage and circumferentially aligned vSMC proliferation were observed. Critically, the PLCL/PU 0.5/0.5 group showed a great patency rate and a desirable functional structure at the 12-week endpoint. These findings present a novel strategy for fabricating small-caliber biocompatible vascular grafts with favorable mechanical properties via a straightforward, continuous single-step process.

title: Chalcogen‐Bridge‐Regulated Proton Shuttling in Tantalum‐Doped Ruthenium Oxide for Robust Acidic Water Oxidation
abstract: ABSTRACT The acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) kinetics on ruthenium dioxide (RuO 2 ) is fundamentally restricted by sluggish deprotonation and interfacial proton transfer. Herein, we introduce chalcogen atoms to tantalum doped RuO 2 (Ta─X─RuO 2 , X = O, S, Se, and Te) and reveal its effects on proton shuttling, including deprotonation and proton transfer from electrocatalyst surface to bulk electrolyte. Significantly, Ta─S─RuO 2 exhibits optimized OER performance due to the balanced hydrogen binding strength of bridge sulfur atoms, promoting deprotonation kinetics and modulating the interfacial water structure to form flexible hydrogen bond network for accelerated proton transfer. Only 1.89 V is demanded for Ta─S─RuO 2 to reach 3 A cm −2 geo and maintains robust performance for 1000 h with voltage decay of 49.0 µV h −1 stemming from the efficient hydrogen bond network to lower the local H + concentration, suppressing the overoxidation of Ru. This work not only reports a novel high‐performance Ta─X─RuO 2 electrocatalysts for acidic OER but also provides new insight into chalcogen‐regulated proton shuttling and promoted OER kinetics and stability, offering guidance to the design of future generation RuO 2 ‐based electrocatalyst.

title: Strategies for Preparing Migration‐Resistant Macromolecular Antioxidants
abstract: ABSTRACT Polymeric materials are susceptible to thermo‐oxidative degradation during melt processing and usage, which can be prevented using antioxidants. However, conventional small‐molecule antioxidants, such as phenolic antioxidants, are prone to migration, which compromises their long‐term effectiveness. To address this, for crystalline/semicrystalline polymers, we propose a systematic design strategy for macromolecular antioxidants based on the “3C principle” (Compatibility, cocrystallization, and crosslinking) to construct novel stabilizers with enhanced antioxidant performance and migration resistance. For noncrystalline polymers, macromolecular antioxidants satisfying only two of these criteria can also provide good antioxidant performance. Based on these design principles, three different types of macromolecular antioxidants were developed with structures tailored to the characteristics of commodity plastics, including polyethylene, polymethyl methacrylate, and polystyrene. This work provides a new approach for enhancing the service stability of polymeric materials and offers a broad molecular design strategy for functionalized polymer materials.
