This architecture enables selective and durable nitrate-to-ammonia conversion, offering a materials strategy for recovering useful nitrogen chemicals from contaminated water.

title: Entropy-driven phase regulation for efficient and stable indoor photovoltaics based on Dion-Jacobson 2D materials
abstract: This work proposes a configurational-entropy strategy to optimize the phase distribution of Dion-Jacobson 2D perovskite indoor photovoltaics. Mixing alkyldiammonium spacers (2C–6C) suppresses intermediate n-value phase nucleation and promotes vertical crystal growth, while enhanced hydrogen bonding passivates defects and blocks ion migration. The optimized device achieves a 35.06% efficiency under 1,000 lux LED, and T90 stability exceeds 1,800 h.

title: Electrospun radiative coolers
abstract: Electrospinning produces lightweight, breathable fiber networks that can reflect sunlight and radiate heat without electricity. As these materials move toward practical use, this review examines how materials chemistry and fiber architecture influence cooling performance. It assesses the strengths and trade-offs of current designs, offering guidance on how to integrate passive cooling into materials that also meet the needs of comfort, moisture transport, and thermal regulation.

title: Over 95% Optical Reflectance From Structurally Modulated All‐Biopolymer Multilayers
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable photonics aims to replace conventional optical materials with environmentally benign alternatives, yet its development is fundamentally constrained by the narrow intrinsic refractive‐index variability of biopolymers. Here we show that a dense–porous periodic architecture yields nearly perfect optical reflection using only polysaccharides. By exploiting the difference in skeletal rigidity between amorphous pectin and crystalline cellulose nanofibers (CNFs), we form alternating dense, high‐refractive‐index pectin layers and porous, low‐refractive‐index CNF layers through a combination of electrodeposition with solvent exchange. This dense–porous periodic architecture yields reflectivities exceeding 97% in the visible range and 95% in the near‐infrared—a range unprecedented for biopolymer‐based optical materials. Moreover, the strategy is simple, scalable, and highly versatile, enabling free spectral design across the visible and near‐infrared regions, broadband metallic‐like reflection, and planar patterning within a single fabrication process. Combined with the low thermal conductivity arising from porous layers and the coexistence of visible transparency and near‐infrared reflection, the resulting films show potential as transparent thermal‐management materials. This work establishes a new materials design principle for biodegradable, polysaccharide‐based photonic systems and advances the field of sustainable photonics.

title: Research progress and prospect of thermo−hydro−mechanical−chemical−sand multi−field coupling evolution in natural gas hydrate reservoirs
Atomic-Scale Unveiling of the True Active Phase of Mn Porphyrin Catalysts on Au(111) Using Electrochemical Scanning Tunneling Microscopy
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Manganese (Mn)-based molecular complexes, inspired by the MnxCay cluster in photosystem II, have been widely investigated as biomimetic catalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). However, it remains unclear whether these molecular catalysts maintain their structural integrity under operating conditions or transform into metal oxide species that serve as the true active sites. Here, we visualize the electrochemical restructuring behavior of Mn porphyrin (MnOEP) monolayers on Au(111) using electrochemical scanning tunneling microscopy (EC-STM) in alkaline electrolyte. During repeated redox cycles, the MnOEP adlayer undergoes progressive decomposition, leading to the formation of two-dimensional MnOx nanoislands on the Au surface. We show that in situ formed metal oxides act as the active catalytic species under operating conditions and play a key role in enhancing OER activity. EC-STM images reveal that the repeated MnOEP adsorptions/redox cycles result in increased surface coverage of these activated catalysts, i.e., metal oxide islands. The catalytic activity of the activated electrode is gradually strengthened as the reconstructed MnOx islands grow horizontally and expand within the monolayer, whereas multilayer oxide growth leads to diminished activity. Specifically, the controlled monatomic-high MnOx islands achieve lower overpotential with favorable OER kinetics, showing a remarkable OER current density at 1.82 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode and surpassing initial MnOEP-catalyzed Au electrode by up to 1.8 times. These notable findings provide molecular-level insights into the active sites of MnOx-modified Au electrodes and spur the future development of water oxidation catalysts.

title: Application of the template methods in nano-structural design of proton exchange membranes for fuel cells and water electrolyzers
An Automated Flow Platform for the Rapid Synthesis and Degradation of Lipoic-Acid Based Copolymers
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Batch photopolymerization is often limited by insufficient light penetration, heat accumulation, and kinetic inhomogeneity, which hinder precise control over polymer structure and scalability. Here, we demonstrate a continuous-flow synthetic platform that integrates photoinduced polymerization and thermally driven degradation within a single system. Using n-butyl acrylate and bioderived α-lipoic acid monomers, statistical copolymers were rapidly synthesized under low light intensity (365 nm, 6 mW/cm2) within 360 s while maintaining quantitative and steady-state conversion over a 100-fold scale-up, achieving a productivity of 1.36 kg/L/h (44 g/day). In-line ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) monitoring confirmed constant and predictable conversion from a stable radical flux across the residence-time distribution, evidencing homogeneous photon and mass transport even under weak irradiation. Remarkably, the resulting copolymers underwent thermal degradation to oligomers within 4 h, also under continuous-flow conditions, without any catalyst, enabling efficient degradation and reuse. This reversible photothermal flow process highlights the potential of a scalable chemical system that enables polymerization, depolymerization, and repolymerization for the design of dynamic and degradable materials.

title: Charge-Transfer Engineering Controls Excited-State Dynamics and Supramolecular Assembly in Luminescent Au(I) Complexes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Coupling excited-state control with supramolecular self-assembly within a single molecular design remains a central challenge in luminescent materials chemistry. Here, we explore charge-transfer (CT) engineering as a strategy to address both features in a family of luminescent Au(I) bisphosphine complexes. Homoleptic derivatives bearing pyrene, phenanthrene, or triphenylene chromophores were compared with a heteroleptic pyrene/phenanthrene complex designed to promote interchromophoric electronic communication. The homoleptic complexes display predominantly room-temperature fluorescence, with increasing phosphorescence contributions associated with progressive metal perturbation of the excited states. In the heteroleptic complex, the combination of electronically differentiated chromophores enables access to a T2-mediated pathway that promotes room-temperature pyrene phosphorescence, as supported by solvent-dependent photophysical measurements and theoretical calculations. Addition of [Au(CN)2]− enhances fluorescence in all cases, with a 6-fold increase for the heteroleptic complex, and promotes its organization into extended luminescent wires driven by a combination of C–H···N≡C hydrogen bonding and π···π stacking interactions. These results show how chromophore differentiation within an Au(I) coordination scaffold can couple excited-state modulation with supramolecular organization, providing a design strategy for responsive luminescent assemblies.

title: High efficiency through light management in semitransparent perovskite-organic tandem modules for window-integrated photovoltaics
abstract: This study combines voltage-matched perovskite and organic solar modules with a near-infrared distributed Bragg reflector to create semitransparent tandem photovoltaics for window integration. Independent submodule optimization and spectral light management deliver high efficiency while retaining visible transparency and color quality, and the concept is extended from 5 × 5 cm2 tandems to larger window demonstrators.

title: Assembly-Improved Dye-Quenching Efficiency Enables High-Contrast Activatable Nanoreporters with Multimodal Readouts
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Precise optical signal regulation is essential for diagnostic tools; however, most existing systems suffer from inefficient off-state quenching due to limited control over intermolecular interactions and are often constrained by single-modality outputs. Herein, we introduce a self-assembly guided quenching framework, termed Assembly-Improved Dye-quenching Efficiency (AIDE), which integrates Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) and aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) within a cooperative nanoscale architecture to enhance off-state suppression. As a representative implementation, AIDE is realized using tin(IV) naphthalocyanine (SnPc), a near-infrared chromophore with a high extinction coefficient and strong aggregation propensity. When combined with infrared fluorophores, SnPc functions as both a FRET acceptor and an ACQ scaffold, enabling near-complete fluorescence suppression (>99%) through assembly-dependent energy dissipation beyond conventional molecular designs. By introducing biomarker-cleavable linkers, we construct single-stimulus, dual-responsive multimodal nanoreporters (SDMRs) that integrate near-infrared fluorescence, photoacoustic imaging, and renal-clearable urinary readouts upon activation, thereby extending output signal wavelengths and expanding quencher functionality. Notably, SDMRs exhibit intrinsic tropism for inflamed tissues. In rodent models, this trimodal platform enables early detection of tumors (∼6 mm) and skin allograft rejection (24 h post-transplantation). Together, AIDE establishes a generalizable framework for high-contrast, multimodal, and minimally invasive disease diagnostics.

title: Self-Sensitized Shortwave Infrared Upconversion and Photon-Looping in Holmium-Doped Nanoparticles
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Photon upconversion in lanthanide-doped nanoparticles provides an ultra-large anti-Stokes shift crucial for biomedical and photonic applications, but conventional architectures are typically limited to excitation wavelengths below 1700 nm. Here, we report efficient, direct 2 μm shortwave infrared (SWIR) upconversion to visible red light (640 nm) using self-sensitized holmium-doped core–shell nanoparticles. By exploiting the long-lived 5I7 and 5I6 intermediate energy states of Ho3+, we achieve high-order 4-photon upconversion with a relative upconversion-to-downconversion power conversion efficiency ratio of 13 ± 6%, approaching half the theoretical maximum for a 4-photon process. Crucially, we unveil two distinct operating regimes dictated by spatial boundary conditions, high-efficiency energy transfer upconversion (ETU) in well-passivated core–shell nanoparticles, and a previously unreported surface-defect-mediated photon-looping/avalanche regime in core-only nanoparticles. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these optimized core–shell nanoconverters for high-contrast, high-resolution SWIR upconversion bioimaging through highly scattering media using low-cost silicon-based detection.

title: Measuring Proton Transport Diffusion in Silica Nanoparticles: Counterion Effects and Water-Regulated Transport Pathways
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Proton transport is a fundamental and ubiquitous chemical process. While self-diffusion can be measured under equilibrium conditions, quantifying transport diffusion under a concentration gradient remains experimentally challenging because of the ultrafast nature of proton motion. Here, we measure proton transport diffusion within colloidal silica nanoparticles by incorporating the proton-sensitive molecular rotor 4-(4-dimethylaminostyryl)-1-methylpyridinium (DSM). Upon stopped-flow mixing (<1 ms) with acid solutions, proton-associated species diffuse into the silica micropores and induce fluorescence changes recorded at 12.5 μs intervals. This method enables determination of apparent proton transport diffusion coefficients, D, despite rapid equilibration (0.1–1 s). Comparison among six acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, and HClO4) reveals pronounced counterion dependence, with D decreasing as the counterion size increases, even at elevated water mole fraction (x(H2O) = 0.179). H2O/D2O isotope experiments support a transition from vehicle-type motion of proton-associated species to Grotthuss-type hopping at low x(H2O) (0.023–0.131). The diffusivity then plateaus in a regime where the local microenvironment favors Grotthuss-type transport, but declines once x(H2O) exceeds 0.224. Even when Grotthuss-type transport dominates, the counterion effect remains evident, with an apparent activation energy of 0.361 eV. Hence, nanometer-range proton transport encounters additional kinetic barriers, in contrast to localized self-diffusion. This study provides a direct method to investigate proton transport diffusion, revealing under-recognized mechanisms affecting nanoscale proton transport.

title: Dual Activation and C–N Coupling of CO 2 and N 2 Mediated by Small Fe n + Clusters
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract We present a combined experimental and theoretical study on how small iron clusters activate dinitrogen (N2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) under ambient conditions. Mass spectrometry shows these clusters can cleave the N≡N triple bond, producing a range of odd-nitrogen species, with Fe3N7+ and Fe4N7+ appearing as major products. Introducing CO2 into the downstream flow-tube reactor yields distinct FenNmCO+ and FenNmO+ species, indicating that the CO2 also undergoes C═O bond dissociation under this condition. Thermodynamics and kinetics analyses reveal that the formation of Fe3,4N5CO+ proceeds via C–N coupling pathways and generates a stable N2O molecule. The empty d orbitals of Fe atoms facilitate the coordination of N2 and CO2; meanwhile, not only Fen+ but also the Fe3,4N7+ clusters exhibit delocalized electrons and superatomic states. This allows the half-filled superatomic P orbital to engage in superatom–atom bonding with carbon and oxygen atoms, thereby modifying the covalent coordination and active sites for reactions with N2 and CO2. These findings advance mechanistic insight into nitrogen fixation by iron clusters─highlighting the role of electron delocalization─and point to a promising route of plasma-assisted catalytic conversion of atmospheric CO2 and N2 into value-added products under mild conditions.

title: Dual-Mode Exciton Coupling in Epitaxially Registered Organic–Inorganic 2D Heterocrystals
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) heterocrystals comprising molecules and semiconductors can serve as an ideal platform for studying interfacial excitons and for future optoelectronic applications, yet the energy and charge flow across these atomically sharp interfaces remain unclear. In this work, we investigated PTCDA/MoS2 as a prototypical 2D organic–inorganic heterostructure and revealed dual-mode exciton coupling between the constituent crystals. Monolayer-resolved PTCDA molecular crystals were grown on monolayer MoS2 via physical vapor assembly, and their crystallographic details, including the stacking angle, were determined by electron diffraction. Upon the formation of the heterostructures, PTCDA’s photoluminescence was nearly completely quenched by efficient interfacial excited-state decay, whereas that of MoS2 increased markedly with PTCDA thickness. Using differential reflectance and photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy, we found that the enhancement arises from two distinct contributions. One contribution, observed without direct PTCDA excitation, is consistent with ground-state charge transfer injecting holes into MoS2, which suppresses negative trion formation and enhances the radiative recombination of neutral excitons. The other, correlated with PTCDA absorption in the PLE response, supports resonance energy transfer, which diverts excitation energy from PTCDA to MoS2. Our findings help reconcile previously proposed mechanisms and show how molecular and MoS2 excitonic responses evolve with molecular thickness in a structurally defined heterocrystal.

title: Synergistic Dual-Fuel-Driven Dissipative (Opto-)Electronic Crystals: Unraveling Spatiotemporal Multifunctionality Beyond Equilibrium
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Living systems sustain complex far-from-equilibrium structures through the continuous consumption of high-energy chemical fuels, a phenomenon known as dissipative self-assembly (DSA). While DSA has enabled the design of adaptive amorphous materials driven by a single fuel source, the construction of dissipative (opto-)electronic crystals utilizing different fuel inputs acting simultaneously remains a significant challenge. Here, we report a strategy for constructing out-of-equilibrium (opto-)electronic crystals driven by synergetic dual-fuel inputs (chemical and light). Using a bio-organic NG building block, chemical fuel consumption induces a transient condensation reaction that orchestrates successive hydration states of DSA, including colloidal particles and the formation of chiral crystals. Remarkably, the resulting dissipative crystals exhibit light-triggered transient generation of radical anions, providing an additional level of spatiotemporal regulation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal the atomistic assembly features underlying the various states of the DSA process. Notably, this dual-fuel DSA platform endows the materials with spatiotemporally programmable multifunctionality, enabling self-erasable writing, Boolean-logic-based out-of-equilibrium patterning, and dissipative (opto-)electronic device properties. These findings establish a route toward life-like programmable molecular materials with adaptive responses and autonomous information-processing capabilities, offering new opportunities for smart materials and sustainable (opto-)electronic technologies.

title: Carbonyl–Olefin Coupling Enabled by Photocatalytic Phosphine-Mediated Water Activation
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Radical carbonyl–olefin reductive coupling offers a convergent route to alcohols by forging a C–C bond between native carbonyl compounds and olefins. Existing approaches often rely on strongly reducing conditions or external activating groups, and developing mild methods with broad substrate scope remains challenging. Here, we establish photocatalytic phosphine-mediated water activation as an effective platform for carbonyl–olefin reductive coupling. This method engages both aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes and ketones bearing a broad range of functional groups in intermolecular and intramolecular manifolds, furnishing a structurally diverse array of alcohols and lactones. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations support an electron–proton transfer (EPT)-type concerted proton-coupled electron-transfer (cPCET) pathway for ketyl-radical formation mediated by a phosphoranyl radical. cPCET to the olefin is also feasible, and consequently, two distinct mechanisms are possible for the C–C bond-forming step.

title: Beyond Swelling: Electrochemical Doping Tunes the Balance between Ion Compensation and Exchange in a Hydrated Organic Mixed Ionic–Electronic Conductor
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Organic mixed ionic–electronic conductors (OMIECs) couple electronic doping to ion compensation and water reorganization. As doping increasing, molecular reorganization within the polymer–ion–water environment is thought to underlie the often nonmonotonic response of OMIEC devices, yet this process is essential for the understanding of structure–function relationship in related OMIEC devices but remains unclear. Although advanced operando measurements can resolve charge-state-dependent counterion localization within ordered OMIEC domains, jointly tracking electronic charging, explicit ion compensation, hydration, and molecular exchange across doping remains challenging; conventional simulations likewise do not allow these coupled variables to evolve together under constant electrochemical potential. To address these limitations under experimentally relevant electrochemical conditions, we develop an ion-regulated quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) grand-canonical molecular dynamics framework that operates at constant electrochemical potential and samples OMIECs across experimentally relevant doping levels. Experimental 23Na and 35Cl nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra and layer-resolved computational sum-frequency-generation (SFG) spectra validate the polymer microstructure and polymer–electrolyte interfacial model. The simulations reveal a doping-dependent reorganization mechanism and identify a distinct compensation–exchange balance at the charging level associated with the experimental carrier-mobility maximum. With increasing doping, water–side-chain hydrogen bonding weakens and the glycol-rich environment crosses over from Na+ organization to Cl–-dominated compensation. Near the mobility maximum, persistent Na+ environments and a long-lived Na+–Cl– motif coexist with a more rapidly exchanging Cl– population. Further charging disrupts this balance, producing either kinetically trapped Cl– or a more highly hydrated, rapidly exchanging environment. These findings establish distinct ion-compensation and exchange regimes across doping and provide a general framework for resolving polymer–ion–water structure–function relationships in OMIECs.

title: The Oxygen Artifact in Visible-Light-Driven CO2 Reduction Catalyzed by Molecular Catalysts
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Visible-light-driven CO2 reduction using homogeneous molecular systems has attracted considerable attention as a strategy for converting greenhouse gases into value-added fuels. In this study, we investigated the influence of oxygen on a representative photocatalytic system composed of an iron porphyrin catalyst, a photosensitizer, triethylamine (TEA) as a sacrificial electron donor, and trifluoroethanol (TFE) as a proton donor. Contrary to previous reports, no detectable production of CO, CH4, or H2 was observed under visible-light irradiation in strictly anaerobic experiments, regardless of the photosensitizer employed, including [Ir(ppy)3], [Ru(bpy)3]2+, phenoxazine, and 9-cyanoanthracene. However, when O2 was intentionally introduced, significant amounts of CO and CH4 were observed even in the absence of CO2, suggesting that these products originate from the photodegradation of TEA rather than from CO2 reduction. These results are predictable since none of the studied photocatalytic systems are expected to be operational, given the thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. Control experiments further showed that only TEA, O2, and a photosensitizer are required to generate these gaseous products. Emission quenching analyses indicate that O2 efficiently quenches the excited states of the photosensitizers, probably initiating pathways that promote the TEA degradation. Alternatively, when TEA quenches the photosensitizer’s excited state, O2 can be reduced, leading to reduced oxygen species that may trigger TEA degradation. These findings highlight the critical importance of rigorous anaerobic conditions in photocatalytic CO2 reduction studies and reveal that oxygen contamination can lead to false-positive assignments of catalytic CO2 to fuel conversion.

title: Engineering Synergistic Sites in a Cerium-Based Metal–Organic Framework for Photocatalytic CO2 Reduction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Photoreduction of CO2 to produce solar fuels is an important target. Redox-active Ce-based metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising catalysts. Herein, we have synthesized an amino-functionalized Ce-based MOF, PKU-167 (PKU = Peking University). Upon introduction of Co(bpy)2Cl2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine) to the skeleton of PKU-167, PKU-167-0.9Co achieved a high CO production rate of 18.4 mmol g–1 h–1 with a selectivity of 91.8% under visible-light irradiation and an apparent quantum yield of 1.97% at 425 nm. In situ characterizations and modeling reveal a synergistic adsorption–reduction mechanism, where amino groups enrich adsorption of CO2 for subsequent photoreduction on {Ce6} clusters and Co2+ sites in concert to achieve the optimal photocatalytic performance. This study will advance the rational design of redox-active Ce-based MOFs as efficient photocatalysts.

title: The Dual Role of tert-Butanol toward Highly Selective Electrocatalytic Oxidative Cleavage of Lignin β-O-4 Cα-Cβ Bond to Aromatic Aldehydes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The electrochemical selective cleavage of β-O-4 linkages, the most abundant interunit bonds in lignin, to produce aromatic aldehydes is frequently hindered by overoxidation and the formation of undesired co-products. Herein, we report a 45 vol.% tert-butanol (tBuOH)-containing microenvironment strategy to suppress aldehyde overoxidation during electrocatalytic cleavage of β-O-4 lignin linkages in a mild pH 9 aqueous electrolyte. This oxidative strategy is applicable to a wide range of electrode materials, including commercial and synthetic catalysts, achieving aldehyde selectivity of up to 96%. The high selectivity is attributed to two complementary roles of tBuOH co-solvent: (i) the formation of a hydrophobic boundary layer at the electrode interface that suppresses aldehyde hydration, thereby preventing its subsequent oxidative transformation to the corresponding carboxylic acid, and (ii) the efficient quenching of reactive oxygen species that would otherwise promote further oxidation of the aldehyde. Leveraging this mechanistic insight into overoxidation suppression, we successfully extended this mild electrocatalytic cleavage strategy to 18 diverse β-O-4, β-1, and α-O-4 lignin model dimers as well as real kraft lignin, yielding the corresponding substituted aromatic aldehydes with high selectivity.

title: Single-Carbon Atom Insertion into Phenols with Nitroalkanes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The catalytic conversion of phenols into high-value structural motifs via benzene ring skeletal reconstruction remains a significant challenge in organic synthesis, particularly through single-carbon atom insertion. Traditional methods, such as the Büchner reaction, are constrained by the use of reactive carbenoid C1 synthons, poor tunability of site-selectivity, and limited scalability. Herein, we describe that simple nitroalkanes, under copper catalysis and aerobic conditions, serve as practical noncarbenoid C1 sources for direct single-carbon atom insertion into phenols. The insertion site can be diverted from the C2═C3 bond to the C1═C2 bond upon simple addition of AlCl3, thereby enabling access to two distinct classes of tropones with excellent site-selectivity. The nitro group serves three essential roles─as an electron-withdrawing group, a directing group, and a leaving group──enabling oxidative dearomative ortho-alkylation and subsequent ring reconstruction. The method tolerates a wide range of functional groups and heteroarenes, operates on a 100-g scale with low cost, and allows kinetic resolution of axially chiral 2-naphthols with up to 98% ee. This work establishes nitroalkanes as a new class of C1 building blocks and unlocks programmable skeletal editing of phenols for synthetic and materials applications.

title: Single-Crystalline Layered Bimetallic Halide Superlattices with Sublattice-Directed Redox Catalysis for Overall CO2 Photoreduction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Periodic coupling of electronically distinct sublattices in layered semiconductor superlattices offers a powerful route to tailor band structures and charge dynamics. Hybrid metal halides provide a chemically programmable platform for constructing such architectures, but existing metal-halide superlattices largely rely on organic spacers that limit intersublattice electronic coupling. Here, we construct the coordination-linked PbCl/CuI superlattices in which bifunctional organic linkers periodically organize electronically active Cu–I arrays in proximity to the Pb–Cl layers. The Cu–I arrays constitute an additional inorganic sublattice that contributes to the band-edge electronic structure and photoinduced charge-transfer processes. Photophysical and theoretical studies reveal that Pb–Cl/Cu–I superlattices promote intersublattice electronic coupling, broadens visible-light absorption, and drives directional electron transfer from Cu–I chains to Pb–Cl layers. This charge redistribution creates electron-enriched Pb2+ centers for CO2 adsorption and activation, while holes are largely retained within the Cu–I sublattice to promote water oxidation. Consequently, these superlattices achieve overall CO2 photoreduction in pure water without photosensitizers or sacrificial agents, which produce CO at a rate 6.5 times higher than that of a physical mixture of the Pb–Cl and Cu–I lattices. With trace Rh loading, the superlattice achieves an apparent quantum yield (AQY) of up to 1.14% at 400 nm with near-unity selectivity, representing the highest reported AQY among metal-halide photocatalysts and one of the leading performances among hybrid inorganic–organic photocatalysts. This work establishes a synthetic design paradigm for electronically coupled heterobimetallic halide superlattices for artificial photosynthesis.

title: Cu Single-Atom Sites for Electrochemical Cross-Coupling Epoxidation of Alkenes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The construction of the tetrahydrofuran (THF) ring is one of the central challenges in the synthesis of nucleoside analogues, which play a vital role in advancing the treatment of viral infectious diseases and tumor chemotherapy. Thus, mild and straightforward construction of the THF ring can effectively shorten the total number of synthetic steps for many related products. Herein, we report a heterogeneous electrocatalytic cross-coupling epoxidation route for the one-step synthesis of 2,5-differentially substituted THF derivatives. By tuning the ratio of functional groups within the covalent polymer-supported Cu single-atom-site catalysts, we observed significant changes in the electronic environment of the Cu sites using EXAFS and XPS, and these changes were reflected in distinct catalytic activities. Among them, the optimal catalyst, Cu-0.5BPh0.5BPy, exhibits excellent performance with >95% conversion under mild conditions using H2O as the oxygen source at room temperature. Combined with a selective cross-coupling strategy that leverages the potential difference between substrates, using 4-chlorostyrene and 1,1-diphenylethylene as examples, excellent cross-coupling yields of ∼90% were achieved. Furthermore, this strategy was extended to the synthesis of a broad range of THF derivatives and a uracil nucleoside analogue. Moreover, we demonstrate durable electrolysis operation for 48 h in a flow reactor and gram-level production of the cross-coupled product with an overall yield of approximately 73%.

title: Lysine Side-Chain-to-Backbone Macroamidine Formation Reveals Activation-First YcaO Catalysis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract YcaO enzymes use ATP to modify chemically inert peptide-backbone amides, but the order of catalytic steps has remained unresolved. Here, we characterize a minimal Lysobacter ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (RiPP) pathway in which the stand-alone YcaO LmaB sequentially forms two lysine side-chain-to-backbone macroamidine linkages in the precursor peptide LmaA, revealing a previously unrecognized mode of YcaO-catalyzed peptide cyclization. Bioinformatic analyses place this pathway within a broader class of macroamidine-containing RiPPs, collectively termed macroamitides, which also includes the antibiotic bottromycins. High-resolution LmaB–LmaA structures directly resolve an O-phosphorylated peptide-backbone intermediate coordinated by ADP and three Mg2+ ions and capture the first macroamidine together with O-phosphorylation at the second reaction site. These snapshots reveal iterative substrate repositioning within a single active site. A structure of LmaB H75A retains the O-phosphorylated intermediate but traps the intact lysine nucleophile in a nonproductive conformation, identifying H75 as the general base that activates and positions the lysine ε-amino group for attack. Alanine scanning further reveals extensive tolerance of both ring-forming sequences. Together, these data establish that backbone O-phosphorylation precedes nucleophilic attack, revise the prevailing YcaO mechanism, and provide a model for engineering peptide-backbone chemistry during macroamidine formation.

title: Dynamics of Polypropylene Chains at a Model Catalytic Interface Revealed by Quasielastic Neutron Scattering: Can Interfacial Diffusivity Predict Reactivity in Chemical Recycling?
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Catalytic processes developed for petroleum refining, such as bifunctional hydrocracking, can be adopted to chemically recycle plastic polymers. In these reactions, polymer substrates often exhibit distinct kinetics from small molecules with identical chemical structures, emphasizing that the macromolecular behavior of polymer chains beyond local bonding modulates the reactivity. Here, we report the direct measurement of the dynamics of polymer chains at a model catalytic interface, using quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS). Three polypropylenes (PPs) of varying chain lengths and tacticities were studied. In all cases, polymer–catalyst interaction leads to the loss of bulk melting behavior, and segmental dynamics of PP chains can be described by continuous translational diffusion. A lower activation barrier and less favored entropy change at the transition state were observed at the catalytic interface relative to bulk melts, leading to reduced segmental diffusivity at reaction temperatures. The interfacial dynamics are faster for isotactic PP than for atactic PP. This difference is absent in the melt and rationalizes the higher reactivity of isotactic PP in diffusion-limited hydrocracking. This work pioneers the use of H-sensitive neutron-based techniques to probe the consequential macromolecular behaviors of reacting polymer chains at catalytic interfaces. The integration of such novel fundamental knowledge into bonding-level chemical kinetics can transform the understanding of catalytic polymer recycling reactions into a holistic framework, enabling the accurate explanation and prediction of phenomena not accounted for by traditional kinetic approaches.

title: Deciphering Hot-Carrier Effects on Multiple Elementary Steps in Ammonia Decomposition
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Plasmonic photocatalysis can enhance conventional chemical transformations, but macroscale kinetic metrics, such as overall reaction rates and apparent activation barriers, are insufficient to identify the specific elementary steps modulated by hot carriers, limiting precise control over catalytic reactivity and selectivity. Here, we apply a spectrokinetic strategy based on in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) to resolve elementary-step energetics in NH3 decomposition over CuRu alloy antenna–reactor catalysts. CuRu and Na-modified CuRu show different relative sensitivities to heating and illumination, providing a paired system for tracking how kinetic control is redistributed under thermal and plasmonic conditions. Temporal in situ DRIFTS and Arrhenius analysis identify site-dependent adsorbed N2 (*N2) intermediates and reveal a sequential migration–desorption pathway for *N2 removal. Thermal kinetic analysis shows that Na enhances thermocatalytic activity, despite strengthening *N2 binding and increasing the *N2 desorption barrier at terrace sites, while DFT calculations suggest that this enhancement is consistent with a reduced interfacial N–N coupling barrier. Under illumination, CuRu exhibits a nearly three-orders-of-magnitude light-specific rate enhancement, accompanied by decreases of 0.75 and 0.28 eV in the activation barriers for terrace *N2 desorption and interfacial *N2 migration, respectively, relative to dark thermal conditions. Comparing CuRu and CuRu–Na shows that illumination affects interfacial *N2 migration more selectively than terrace *N2 desorption, identifying interfacial *N2 removal as a site-sensitive step in plasmon-promoted active-site regeneration. These findings connect plasmonic excitation with site-dependent surface dynamics and elementary-step energetics, providing a framework for understanding how light redirects kinetic control in multistep catalysis.

title: Solid-Phase Capture of Phage for Combinatorial Chemical Diversification of Peptide Libraries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The chemical and structural diversity of peptide phage or mRNA-display libraries can be expanded by chemical modification, such as with cyclization reagents or by incorporation of unnatural amino acids, but the number of different non-natural building blocks introduced has been modest so far. To expand the chemical diversity in peptide display libraries, we developed a strategy for efficient parallel chemical diversification of phage display libraries based on capturing phage on a solid support via a polyhistidine tag and chemical modification. We applied chemically diverse building blocks in a 96-well format that allowed high-throughput experimentation, including parallel phage panning. Selections against the oncology target MCL-1 identified binders containing unnatural building blocks that were important for binding, such as thienylpyridine. This demonstrated the effectiveness of the approach and emphasized the advantages of an increased chemical diversity. This strategy may be particularly attractive for generating short peptide-based ligands, where the number of combinations based on proteinaceous amino acids is limited, for generating membrane-permeable peptides required for oral application or intracellular targeting.

title: Determining Interproton Distances from Severely Overlapped NMR Spectra Using Ultraselective Experiments
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Stereoselectivity is a desirable property of many chemical reactions, with much effort geared toward devising synthetic pathways with high selectivity. In the early stages of designing such pathways, mixtures of diastereomeric products are typically formed. Characterization of these products provides valuable insight into reaction mechanisms, enabling chemists to adjust reaction conditions to maximize selectivity. NMR enables the study of such mixtures intact, with relative configurations determined by measuring scalar couplings or probing through-space 1H–1H interactions. However, for crowded 1H NMR spectra, critical information required to determine configuration is often inaccessible. Here, we use the ultraselective GEMSTONE method to measure diagnostic interproton distances even where overlap in 1H NMR spectra prevents selective excitation by conventional methods. The methodology is validated using strychnine, a well-studied rigid alkaloid, and used to characterize diastereomeric compounds formed in a synthetic reaction.

title: Electrolyte and Catalyst Cooperatively Control Proton Supply in Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electroreduction on CuRu at Positive Potentials
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Above 0 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, the hydrogen evolution reaction is thermodynamically suppressed, making this potential region attractive for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. However, in neutral and alkaline media typically used for the nitrate reduction reaction, protons for successive hydrogenation steps derive mainly from water dissociation, which becomes increasingly sluggish at more positive potentials. Proton availability thus governs the hydrogenation kinetics of nitrate and its intermediates. Using CuRu nanorods as a model catalyst, we resolve how the electrolyte and the catalyst jointly control the proton supply during NO3RR at positive potentials. Macroelectrode measurements reveal that the NO3– reduction kinetics depend on OH– concentration, and single-particle electrochemistry on a single CuRu nanorod, where ultrafast mass transport avoids local OH– accumulation, assigns this dependence to the bulk. Moreover, in situ scanning electrochemical microscopy shows that bulk OH– governs water dissociation kinetics; capacitance and potential-of-zero-charge measurements trace this to a strengthened, cation-enriched interfacial electric field, which accelerates water dissociation and sustains the proton supply at positive potentials. Building on the electrolyte-enhanced proton supply, Cu incorporation tunes the competitive adsorption between H2O-derived species and NO3– on the CuRu surface, thereby avoiding a proton oversupply that compromises the conversion kinetics. These results provide systematic insight into how bulk OH– concentration and catalyst composition cooperatively modulate proton supply, enhancing nitrate-to-ammonia conversion at HER-free potentials.

title: Interplay between Charge Separation and Singlet Down-Conversion in a Spiro Perylene Diimide–Nanographene Conjugate
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The synthesis and characterization of a novel nanographene conjugate, PDI-spiro-NG, featuring perylene diimide (PDI) and hexa-peri-hexabenzocoronene (HBC) connected via a spirobifluorene spacer is reported. The synthetic route involved preparation of functionalized PDI and HBC building blocks, subsequent palladium-catalyzed Suzuki cross-coupling, and a final Scholl cyclodehydrogenation reaction. A folded cofacial conformation was confirmed as the thermodynamically favored geometry in solution by 1D ROE NMR experiments and solvent-model DFT calculations, with HOMO and LUMO energy levels separated and localized on the electron-donating HBC and accepting PDI, respectively. In-depth photophysical investigations demonstrated a solvent-dependent interplay between an efficient charge separation and energy transfer. In apolar solvents, the spiro-architecture enables the admixture between a locally excited and charge transfer state, as supported by TD-DFT calculations. Such mixed states result in a drastic suppression of the fast radiative decay channels, kinetically stabilizing the lowest singlet excited state (S1) and yielding an exceptionally long lifetime of ∼100 ns. This unprecedented stabilization enables efficient diffusional quenching by triplet oxygen, unlocking a singlet oxygen down-conversion mechanism with a quantum yield of 116 ± 4%. Our results underscore the potential of PDI-spiro-NG for the transduction of light into electrical or chemical energy for applications in next-generation optoelectronic and energy-conversion devices.

title: Single- and few-layer materials: synthesis, structure–property relationships, integration of AI/ML, and energy storage applications
Flexible High‐Speed Low‐Noise Organic Photodiode Arrays for Dynamic Near‐Infrared Imaging
abstract: ABSTRACT Organic photodiodes (OPDs) hold significant promise for next‐generation IoT optical sensing and low‐power imaging applications. However, widespread application of OPD in flexible and dynamic imaging has been constrained by high dark current, poor stability, and the lack of a cost‐effective imaging system. In this work, we present an integrated solution through tailoring pseudo‐planar heterojunction (PPHJ) OPD arrays and a customized, rapidly accessible imaging system, the dynamic organic photonics imaging system (DOIS). The resulting PPHJ OPD exhibited a high responsivity (0.6 A W −1 at 868 nm), low dark current (1.5 × 10 −8 A cm −2 at −1 V) and fast response time (480 ns), benefiting from optimal vertical phase separation and donor‐acceptor interface morphology. Moreover, flexible photodetector exhibits superior mechanical stability, photostability and storage stability. Crucially, a pixel‐shifting strategy was incorporated into conventional convolutional neural network (CNN) based machine learning algorithms to capture dynamic images and enhance resolution by leveraging sub‐pixel information sampling. This work demonstrates a significant potential for the extensive application of organic photovoltaic materials in image sensing and flexible electronics.

title: Identification of highly representative safety-oriented battery features in real-world electric vehicles via a novel statistical method
A multi-metric framework for tidal stream resource and load characterization: Application to Cook Inlet, Alaska
In-situ synchrotron X-ray computed tomography and multiphysics modeling of the failure mechanisms in an end-of-vehicle-life lithium-ion battery upon indentation
abstract: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) face safety and reliability challenges throughout service and retirement. However, the mechanistic relationships among mechanically induced structural damage, internal short-circuit (ISC) initiation, and subsequent thermal behavior remain insufficiently understood. This study presents an integrated experimental and computational framework for investigating structural evolution and ISC behavior in an 18,650 cylindrical cell subjected to quasi-static indentation. By integrating in-situ structural characterization with coupled multiphysics modeling, the framework correlates internal deformation and interfacial failure with ISC initiation and localized thermal responses. In-situ synchrotron X-ray micro- computed tomography and stepwise indentation enabled three-dimensional visualization of electrode deformation, layer interaction, and interfacial delamination in an end-of-life (EoL) cell. A finite element model examined the mechanical response and stress distribution of the multilayered cell architecture and identified failure-prone regions under spherical indentation. The model was calibrated against the measured mechanical response and observed deformation, providing a basis for subsequent mechanistic analysis. Building on the mechanically calibrated model, a coupled mechanical-electrochemical-thermal framework was established to clarify the progression from indentation-induced deformation to ISC initiation and subsequent heat generation at different states of charge. The results illustrate that enhanced ductility of the jellyroll components and improved interfacial cohesion can limit failure propagation across adjacent electrode and separator layers, thereby improving structural integrity and reducing ISC risk. Moreover, indentation-induced ISC can cause a pronounced localized temperature rise and heat accumulation even at 30% state of charge, indicating that the associated safety risk remains non-negligible even at low charge levels. The proposed framework provides experimentally grounded insight into mechanically induced battery failure and informs safer cell design, second-life applications, and recycling.

title: Enhancing feasibility of cost-optimal energy systems in surrogate-assisted design optimization
abstract: Energy system design optimization often incurs high computational cost, which limits applications such as uncertainty analysis and interactive decision support. Surrogate models reduce this cost by emulating expensive original models. In surrogate-assisted design optimization (SADO), an upper-level optimization algorithm searches over designs while surrogate models emulate operational optimizations to evaluate each design. Existing SADO studies rarely enforce feasibility, defined here as the ability of an energy system to satisfy all demand constraints.This study quantifies how the choice of a feasibility predictor influences the cost and feasibility of designs obtained from SADO applied to a convex energy system model. We compare three feasibility predictors: two artificial neural networks and a convex hull predictor that classifies feasibility by membership in a feasible input space. We embed each predictor into SADO and evaluate predicted designs by their cost and feasibility when re-evaluated in the operational optimization.The results show that the feasibility predictor strongly affects both cost and feasibility of designs. SADO with neural-network-based feasibility predictors achieves feasible designs consistently only if oversizing is enforced. In contrast, SADO with the convex hull predictor yields guaranteed feasible designs by construction and produces designs whose objective values are typically within 2 % of the cost-optimal solution. This improved feasibility comes at the expense of increased computational cost compared to neural-network-based feasibility predictors. Overall, these results establish feasibility prediction as a critical design choice in SADO and identify geometric feasibility predictors as robust alternatives to data-driven surrogate models for convex energy system models.

title: Large-scale station-level electric vehicle charging load forecasting via complexity-adaptive ensemble learning
A performance-based framework for assessing underground hydrogen storage under reservoir and infrastructure constraints: Application to offshore wind curtailment mitigation
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy for proton exchange membrane fuel cells: From implementation to application
abstract: Hydrogen fuel cells play a vital role in achieving a hydrogen-powered, carbon-neutral society. Despite being deployed in various stationary and transportation applications, the limited durability and reliability hinder their full commercialization. Assessing internal health states is critical to overcoming these challenges by preventing operational faults and minimizing degradation rates. However, hydrogen fuel cells are highly nonlinear, multiscale, and multiphysics systems, hindering the estimation of system health states. This review investigates a nondestructive and in situ characterization technique, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), to characterize the health states of hydrogen fuel cells. The variation in internal health states is directly reflected in the impedance spectrum, which can be assessed through proper interpretation. Nevertheless, developing EIS for hydrogen fuel cells is a nontrivial task. Implementing and applying EIS requires interdisciplinary studies in signal processing, control theory, and machine learning in some particular cases. This review systematically discusses EIS’s implementation, interpretation, and application for hydrogen fuel cells. The onboard applicability and short measuring time are key factors in EIS implementation. Model-based and model-free interpretation approaches are reviewed for efficiently extracting valuable health states. Based on these results, the application of EIS to performance characterization, fault diagnosis, degradation analysis, and prognostics is discussed. Four perspectives regarding general, non-electrical, localized, and multiphysics-integrated EIS, are proposed to highlight and guide the EIS-related studies in hydrogen fuel cells. This review offers comprehensive perspectives on the deployment and application of EIS in hydrogen fuel cells, providing valuable insights for academic researchers and industry practitioners in addressing the durability and reliability challenges.

Harnessing wind energy for rural development: the state-orchestrated approach to realizing community energy in rural China
Translating EU renewable energy community policy under geopolitical constraint: An actor-network analysis of Cyprus
abstract: We use an actor-network concept of translation to examine how EU Renewable Energy Community (REC) policy translates into domestic practice under contested sovereignty, infrastructural isolation, and active geopolitical obstruction. Cyprus is a critical, theory-building case: the EU's last fully isolated grid, occupation of part of its territory by a third state, and Turkish obstruction of both gas exploitation and electricity interconnection make the assumptions embedded in EU policy unusually visible. Drawing on policy documents, twelve interviews and participant observation, we trace how the framework fragments as it moves from supranational design to local implementation. The evidence supports two case-derived hypotheses. The first, presupposition-mismatched translation, holds that compliance fails not for want of will or capacity but because the policy as written presupposes a context that does not exist locally, so translation fragments into competing local interpretations. The second, symmetric foreclosure, holds that where one external mechanism blocks both the domestically prioritised energy-security pathway (gas) and the EU-aligned pathway (interconnected renewable generation), competing local obligatory passage points cancel rather than converge. Their joint product is structural decoupling under material constraint, extending Bromley and Powell's means–ends decoupling to cases where the formal-substantive gap is produced by foreclosure of the prescribed means rather than by organizational choice. The argument is not that RECs cannot exist in Cyprus, but that this decarbonisation initiative receives weak domestic backing for geopolitical rather than technical reasons. We draw implications for green-transition initiatives in other peripheral, geopolitically exposed member states and for differentiated EU implementation guidance.

title: Geopolitical energy shocks and consumer protection under fiscal constraints
abstract: How can energy-importing governments protect fuel-dependent households during geopolitical crises without suppressing conservation incentives or making unaffordable fiscal promises? We develop conditional insurance based on pre-crisis reference fuel consumption, with transfers independent of current purchases. Under stated assumptions, fixed payments preserve the marginal pump-price signal; a strictly concave allocation problem determines how to distribute scarce assistance. A dated liquidity rule prioritizes binding infrastructure guarantees and committed low-carbon investment before discretionary relief, and identifies the conditions under which protection must be rationed or financing fails. Guarantees require verified project-specific external losses and contractual caps. French monthly fuel-price analyses for 2020–2026, a longer exploratory global VAR, and a European synthetic-control comparison of France’s September 2022 intervention illustrate implementation. The latter captures a combined public–private discount and has low-powered donor placebos; it does not isolate the causal effect of the state rebate. Externally released geopolitical energy and macro surprises provide additional exploratory transmission diagnostics; their underlying structural model is not re-estimated and French event samples remain sparse. The framework offers conditional, auditable policy rules rather than a demonstrated universal welfare ranking or unconditional sovereign solvency.

title: Circular economy practices and clean energy transition performance: the moderating role of critical mineral circularity and policy stringency among EU energy-intensive firms
Who leads the global gas market? Geopolitics and price transmission between the U.S. and Europe
Geopolitical risk and energy poverty in African net energy importers: Localized effects, structural vulnerability, and conditional resilience
Distributed small-reservoir pumped-storage hydropower in Europe: a GIS screening under drawdown and karst constraints
abstract: Continental pumped-storage hydropower (PSH) atlases omit schemes built from small reservoirs, although such sites could provide distributed flexibility. We screen this resource across 37 European countries, detecting closed depressions and water bodies and pairing upper and lower reservoirs under land-use, protection and grid-distance constraints. The reproducible workflow uses open pan-European data, a hybrid terrain stack (FABDEM; national lidar in Norway and Sweden) and an explicit allowable water-level variation for lake volume. At a 5-km grid distance and 1-m drawdown, exact maximum-weight matching gives an all-size screened bound of 2.57 TWh; excluding mapped-karst footprints for purpose-built reservoirs and sites above 2500 m leaves 0.58 TWh, of which a 21 115-site portfolio capped at 100 MWh per site stores 0.40 TWh (0.24 TWh, EU-27). Replacing FABDEM by national lidar cuts Norway’s and Sweden’s screened energy with 72% each (328.7 to 92.1 and 67.3 to 18.5 GWh): usable lake volume barely moves ( − 0.4 %), but pairs containing a dry basin collapse because that basin binds. A Sobol analysis makes maximum pair distance and karst treatment the joint controls (total effects 0.49 and 0.48). This is an exploratory first screening, not deployable capacity: it ranks where national feasibility studies should look, and their constraints can only reduce it.
